title: Generics
scopeHtml: Scope: invariance, out/in variance (declaration-site and use-site), star projections, type erasure and reified, upper bounds and where, generic nullability, @UnsafeVariance, List vs MutableList variance, arrays, generic inference, and Nothing as the bottom type. Inline mechanics in general, @JvmSuppressWildcards, and read-only vs immutable collections are covered in their own chunks.

questions.promptHtml: String is a subtype of Any. Why can't I pass a MutableList<String> to a function that takes a MutableList<Any>?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the entry point to all variance questions. They want to see if you know subtyping of generic types is a separate rule from subtyping of their arguments, and if you can explain why with a concrete counterexample.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Generic types in Kotlin are invariant by default. MutableList<String> and MutableList<Any> have no subtype relationship, even though String is a subtype of Any. If the compiler allowed it, the function could call add(42) on what it thinks is a list of Any. That would put an Int into a list the caller still holds as MutableList<String>, and the caller would crash with a ClassCastException later, far from the bug. Invariance is the compiler refusing to let that happen. Java has the same rule: List<String> is not a List<Object>.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two different relationships get mixed up:

  • Subclassing: ArrayList<String> is a subtype of MutableList<String>, because ArrayList implements MutableList. This goes through the class hierarchy and always works.
  • Subtyping across type arguments: is Box<Dog> a subtype of Box<Animal>? That depends on the variance of Box's type parameter. The default answer is no.

Why no is the safe default: a type parameter can show up in two kinds of positions.

class Box<T> {
    fun get(): T          // T in "out" position: Box hands T out
    fun set(value: T)     // T in "in" position: Box takes T in
}

If Box<Dog> were a Box<Animal>:
    val animals: Box<Animal> = dogBox
    animals.set(Cat())        // compiles: Cat is an Animal
    val d: Dog = dogBox.get() // runtime: it's a Cat -> ClassCastException

Reading is safe in one direction, and writing is safe in the opposite direction. A type that does both can only be safe if it's invariant. Kotlin gives you out and in to relax invariance when a type only reads or only writes (see the next question).

At runtime there is only one ArrayList class. The type argument is erased, so the JVM would not stop the bad add. The crash only happens when someone reads the element back and the compiler-inserted checkcast String fails. That's why the compiler has to enforce this statically.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun addDefaults(target: MutableList<Any>) {
    target.add(42)
}

val names: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("a")
// addDefaults(names)          // compile error: type mismatch

// Fix 1: the function only reads -> accept a read-only, covariant List
fun printAll(items: List<Any>) = items.forEach(::println)
printAll(names)                 // OK, List<out E> is covariant

// Fix 2: the function only writes Strings -> use-site 'in' projection
fun addDefaultName(target: MutableList<in String>) { target.add("unknown") }
addDefaultName(names)           // OK

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "Kotlin generics are covariant" because List<String> is assignable to List<Any>. That works because List is declared out E. MutableList isn't.
  • Escaping the compile error with names as MutableList<Any>. That's an unchecked cast that pollutes the list, and it always "succeeds" because of erasure.
  • Confusing subclassing (ArrayList<T> : MutableList<T>) with variance. They're independent.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Array<String> an Array<Any>? → No. Kotlin arrays are invariant, unlike Java's covariant arrays (see Q143).
  2. Why does val x: List<Any> = listOf("a") compile? → List is declared List<out E>, so it's covariant.
  3. Could the JVM catch the bad add at runtime? → No. Generic arguments are erased, so add(Object) accepts anything. Only arrays carry a runtime element type, which is why Java arrays throw ArrayStoreException and Java lists don't.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "generics are invariant, it's a compile error." The senior answer gives the read/write counterexample, explains that erasure means the runtime can't help, and fixes the API by asking what the function actually does: reads only → List<T> or out; writes only → in.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The common bug isn't the compile error. It's the "fix": a cast to MutableList<Any> that a later change exploits, and a ClassCastException in an unrelated screen weeks later.

questions.promptHtml: Explain out and in in Kotlin generics. When do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the most common generics question. They're checking that you can derive the rule from positions instead of reciting "producer out, consumer in."

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: out T makes a type covariant: if Dog is an Animal, then Producer<Dog> is a Producer<Animal>. The price is that T can only appear in output positions, like return types and vals. in T makes it contravariant: Consumer<Animal> is a Consumer<Dog>, and T can only appear in input positions, like parameters. The rule of thumb is "producer out, consumer in." Kotlin's List<out E> is covariant and Comparable<in T> is contravariant. The compiler checks every member against the declared variance.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Dog <: Animal
 out (covariant)      Source<Dog>    <: Source<Animal>      same direction
 in  (contravariant)  Sink<Animal>   <: Sink<Dog>           reversed direction
 invariant            Box<Dog>  and  Box<Animal>            unrelated

Why each is safe:

  • A Source<Dog> only ever returns Dogs. Anyone expecting a Source<Animal> receives Dogs, and Dogs are Animals. Nothing breaks.
  • A Sink<Animal> can accept any Animal. Anyone holding it as a Sink<Dog> will only give it Dogs, and it can handle those. Nothing breaks.

Position rules the compiler enforces for out T:

  • Allowed: return types, val property types, type arguments of other out types in return position (for example fun all(): List<T>).
  • Rejected: function parameter types and var properties, because a var has a setter, which is an input.

For in T it's the mirror image: parameters are allowed, and return types are rejected.

Real stdlib examples:

Declaration Variance Why
interface List<out E> covariant read-only API, only returns E
interface Comparable<in T> contravariant only takes T in compareTo(other: T)
interface MutableList<E> invariant both get(): E and add(E)
Function1<in P, out R> both takes P, returns R

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Source<out T> {
    fun next(): T
    // fun push(item: T)      // error: T is declared 'out' but occurs in 'in' position
}

interface Sink<in T> {
    fun accept(item: T)
    // fun last(): T          // error: T is declared 'in' but occurs in 'out' position
}

open class Animal
class Dog : Animal()

fun demo(dogs: Source<Dog>, animalSink: Sink<Animal>) {
    val animals: Source<Animal> = dogs       // OK: covariance
    val dogSink: Sink<Dog> = animalSink      // OK: contravariance
    dogSink.accept(Dog())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking out means "read-only object" or "immutable." It only restricts where T appears in the type's own API. The implementation can still be mutable internally.
  • Getting contravariance's direction backwards. Anchor it with Comparator<Any>: a comparator that can compare any two objects can certainly compare two Strings.
  • Forgetting that a var property is both an input and an output, so it forces invariance.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Map this to Java. → out T ≈ ? extends T, in T ≈ ? super T. Java's PECS ("Producer Extends, Consumer Super") is the same rule.
  2. Why can List<out E> have contains(element: E)? → It's annotated @UnsafeVariance, because contains doesn't store the element (see Q147).
  3. Can one class be out in one parameter and in in another? → Yes. Function1<in P, out R> is exactly that, and it's why (Any) -> String is assignable to (String) -> Any.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer recites "producer out, consumer in." The senior answer explains why it's sound with the "anyone expecting X receives Y" argument, names stdlib examples on both sides, and knows the compiler checks positions, including the var rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Domain interfaces declared invariant by default (Repository<T>, Mapper<I, O>) force callers into casts or duplicated code. Declaring Mapper<in I, out O> once removes a whole class of "type mismatch" workarounds.

questions.promptHtml: Why is List<String> assignable to List<Any> but MutableList<String> isn't assignable to MutableList<Any>?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you connect a familiar everyday behavior to declaration-site variance, and whether you know the caveat that List is read-only, not immutable.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Because of how they're declared. kotlin.collections.List is List<out E>, so it's covariant. Its API only hands E out: get, first, iteration. MutableList<E> adds add(E) and set(index, E), which take E in, so it has to be invariant. Both are the same java.util.List at runtime. The variance exists only in Kotlin's type system. That's a compile-time view of the object, not a property of the object itself.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kotlin maps java.util.List to two Kotlin interfaces:

            Collection<out E>           (read-only, covariant)
                   |
             List<out E>                (get, indexOf, subList ... all output)
                   |
          MutableList<E>                (add, set, removeAt ... input too -> invariant)
                   |
        ArrayList<E> (java.util.ArrayList at runtime)

Consequences:

  1. List<Dog> → List<Animal> is free. That's why returning List<T> from a repository is the ergonomic choice. Callers can widen it without copying.
  2. MutableList<Dog> → MutableList<Animal> is rejected, because you could add(Cat()).
  3. MutableList<Dog> → List<Animal> is fine. You go up to List<Dog> (an interface supertype), then widen covariantly.
  4. Some read methods mention E as a parameter: contains(element: E), indexOf(element: E). These would violate out, so the stdlib marks them @UnsafeVariance. They don't store the argument, so it's still sound.

The caveat: covariance is about what this reference can do. A List<Animal> you received may be backed by a MutableList<Dog> someone else still mutates. Read-only is not immutable (see the collections chunk).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
open class Animal
class Dog : Animal()
class Cat : Animal()

val dogs: MutableList<Dog> = mutableListOf(Dog())

val ro: List<Animal> = dogs              // OK: MutableList<Dog> <: List<Dog> <: List<Animal>
// val rw: MutableList<Animal> = dogs    // error

// What the compiler is preventing:
@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
val polluted = dogs as MutableList<Animal>   // compiles with a warning, no runtime check
polluted.add(Cat())
// val d: Dog = dogs[1]                  // ClassCastException: Cat cannot be cast to Dog

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying List is covariant "because it's immutable." It's covariant because its API is output-only. Immutability is a different guarantee, and Kotlin's List doesn't provide it.
  • Exposing MutableList<T> from a class "for flexibility." Callers lose covariance, and they can mutate your state.
  • Assuming contains(Any) works on List<String> without thought. listOf("a").contains(1) doesn't compile, because the parameter type is E. There's a stdlib extension Iterable<T>.contains(element: T) with an @kotlin.internal.OnlyInputTypes annotation that controls this. Use any { it == x } for mixed types.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Java see for a Kotlin function parameter List<Animal>? → List<? extends Animal>, because Kotlin emits wildcards for covariant parameters (unless the argument type is final). See the interop chunk for @JvmSuppressWildcards.
  2. Is Map<K, V> covariant? → Map<K, out V>. Keys are invariant because get(key: K) and containsKey(key: K) take K in.
  3. Why not make MutableList out with @UnsafeVariance on add? → add stores the element, so that annotation would enable exactly the heap pollution variance prevents.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "List is immutable, MutableList isn't." The senior answer says it's declaration-site out E on a read-only view, names the @UnsafeVariance exceptions, and points out the read-only-isn't-immutable trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that expose MutableList from ViewModels or repositories end up with UI-thread mutation bugs and lose the free widening. Expose List<T> and keep the mutable list private.

questions.promptHtml: What is type erasure, and what can't you do in Kotlin on the JVM because of it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Erasure explains a whole family of production bugs (Gson LinkedTreeMap, unchecked casts, overload clashes). They want to see that you know what's erased and what isn't.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On the JVM, generic type arguments exist only at compile time. After type checking, List<String> and List<Int> both compile down to plain java.util.List, and the compiler inserts casts where values come out. So at runtime I can't ask x is List<String>, can't write T::class or is T in a normal generic function, and can't overload two functions that differ only in type arguments. What survives are declared signatures in class metadata, which is what reflection-based libraries like Gson and Retrofit read. The escape hatches are reified type parameters on inline functions, or passing a Class/KClass/KType explicitly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why: Java added generics in Java 5 while keeping binary compatibility with pre-generics bytecode, so the JVM never learned about type arguments. Kotlin/JVM inherits that.

What the compiler does:

Source:   val first: String = names[0]        // names: List<String>
Bytecode: INVOKEINTERFACE java/util/List.get(I)Ljava/lang/Object;
          CHECKCAST java/lang/String          // cast inserted at the use site
Erased (not available at runtime) Kept (in class file Signature attributes)
Type arguments of local variables and expressions Generic signatures of class declarations, superclasses, fields, method params/returns
T inside a generic function body Kotlin @Metadata (nullability, declaration-site variance)
Which List<?> an object was created as Array element class (String[] vs Object[])

What you can't do, and the compiler messages you'll see:

  • x is List<String> → "Cannot check for instance of erased type." x is List<*> is fine.
  • if (x is T) in a non-reified function → same error.
  • x as List<String> → compiles with an "Unchecked cast" warning and checks only List.
  • fun f(a: List<String>) and fun f(a: List<Int>) in one class → "Platform declaration clash" (both erase to f(Ljava/util/List;)V). The interop chunk covers fixing it with @JvmName.
  • T() or arrayOf<T>() in a non-reified function → not allowed.

One subtlety: Kotlin allows is ArrayList<String> when the static type already fixes the argument. For example, if x: List<String>, then x is ArrayList<String> compiles, because only the class part needs a runtime check.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun describe(x: Any) = when (x) {
    // is List<String> -> ...        // error: erased type
    is List<*> -> "list of ${x.size}" // OK: star projection, checks only the class
    else -> "other"
}

fun narrow(xs: List<String>) {
    if (xs is ArrayList<String>) xs.ensureCapacity(100) // OK: argument known statically
}

// Reified as the workaround:
inline fun <reified T> Iterable<*>.firstOfType(): T? = firstOrNull { it is T } as T?

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing an unchecked as List<User> validates elements. It checks only that the object is a List, and the crash comes later at checkcast User.
  • Thinking erasure means "no generic info anywhere." Declaration signatures survive, and that's how super-type tokens work (see Q150).
  • Assuming Kotlin/Native or JS behave identically. This question is about the JVM. Don't generalize without checking.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where exactly does the ClassCastException get thrown? → At the compiler-inserted checkcast in the caller that reads the element as a concrete type, not at the cast that caused it.
  2. How does reified get around erasure? → The function is inlined, and the compiler substitutes the concrete type at each call site (Q144).
  3. Why do arrays know their element type? → JVM arrays are reified objects ([Ljava/lang/String;). Only the element class is kept, so Array<List<String>> is still List[] at runtime.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "generics are removed at runtime." The senior answer explains checkcast placement, which explains where the crash shows up, separates erased expression types from preserved declaration signatures, and lists the escape hatches with their trade-offs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Almost every "LinkedTreeMap cannot be cast to X" crash in Android is erasure plus a reflection-based JSON library given a raw Class instead of a full Type.

questions.promptHtml: How do upper bounds work in Kotlin generics, and when do you need a where clause?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks basic generic-function fluency and whether you know the less obvious details: the implicit Any? bound, the single-class-bound rule, and JVM erasure to the first bound.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: <T : Number> restricts T to Number or its subtypes, so inside the function I can call Number members on a T. With no bound, the implicit bound is Any?, so T may be nullable. When I need more than one bound, for example "a CharSequence that's also Comparable to itself," I use where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T>. Only one bound can be a class. The rest must be interfaces. On the JVM, the parameter erases to the first bound, which matters for Java interop and reflection.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf3(a: T, b: T, c: T): T = maxOf(a, maxOf(b, c))

fun <T> longestSorted(items: List<T>): List<T>
    where T : CharSequence,
          T : Comparable<T> =
    items.sorted().sortedByDescending { it.length }

Rules:

  1. Default bound is Any?. fun <T> f(t: T) accepts null. Write <T : Any> to forbid it (Q145).
  2. One class bound at most. You can't write where T : View, T : Fragment. A class bound must be first in practice, and Kotlin rejects two class bounds.
  3. Erasure goes to the first bound. In where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T>, the JVM signature uses CharSequence, and calls to compareTo get a checkcast Comparable. Reordering bounds changes the JVM method descriptor, which is a binary-compatibility change for a published library.
  4. Bounds on classes work the same way: class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>.
  5. Recursive bounds like T : Comparable<T> express "comparable to its own kind." Q151 covers self-types in depth.

Bounds are checked at the call site. maxOf3(1, 2, 3) infers T = Int. maxOf3(1, "a", 2) fails, because no single T satisfies Comparable<T>.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Without the bound, `it.length` doesn't compile because T could be anything.
fun <T : CharSequence> totalLength(xs: List<T>): Int = xs.sumOf { it.length }

// Android example: a bound lets generic code use the class's API.
fun <V : android.view.View> android.view.View.requireChild(id: Int): V =
    findViewById<V>(id) ?: error("No view with id $id")

// Two bounds: one class + one interface, class first.
fun <T> attach(view: T) where T : android.view.View, T : Runnable {
    view.post(view)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing fun <T> f(x: T) { x.hashCode() } and thinking T can't be null. It can, and hashCode() works only because there's an Any?.hashCode() extension.
  • Putting where constraints on a type parameter that's also constrained inline (<T : A> ... where T : B). That's a compile error. Put all bounds in where.
  • Treating a bound as a runtime check. It's compile-time only. A Java caller passing a raw type can still violate it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does fun <T : Number> f(t: T) look like in bytecode? → f(Ljava/lang/Number;)V. The parameter type is the erasure of the bound.
  2. Can a bound reference another type parameter? → Yes: fun <T, R : T> f(...) or fun <K, M : MutableMap<in K, *>>.
  3. Why can't you have two class bounds? → The JVM has single inheritance, so no class could satisfy both unless one extends the other, and then one bound is redundant.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer covers <T : X> and where syntax. The senior answer adds the implicit Any? bound, erasure to the first bound and its binary-compatibility implication, and that bounds are compile-time only.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: In shared libraries, reordering where bounds or tightening a bound looks like a harmless refactor. It changes the erased JVM descriptor and breaks already-compiled consumers with NoSuchMethodError.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between declaration-site and use-site variance in Kotlin? When do you need type projections?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most candidates know out/in on interfaces. Fewer know projections like Array<out Any> or MutableList<in T>, and fewer still can say what members become unusable on a projected type.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Declaration-site variance is when the class itself is declared out T or in T, like List<out E>. Every use is covariant automatically. Use-site variance is for invariant classes like MutableList or Array that both read and write T. At a specific use I write MutableList<out Number> or MutableList<in Int>, which is called a type projection. A projection restricts what I can call through that reference. out lets me read but turns add into "takes Nothing," and in lets me write but reading gives me Any?. It's Java's ? extends / ? super, but Kotlin lets you declare variance once on the type, so you need projections less often.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Java has only use-site variance, which is why Java signatures are full of List<? extends T>. Kotlin adds declaration-site variance for types that are naturally one-directional, and keeps projections for the rest.

What a projection does to member signatures of MutableList<E>:

Member MutableList<Number> MutableList<out Number> MutableList<in Number>
get(i): E returns Number returns Number returns Any?
add(e: E) takes Number takes Nothing (uncallable) takes Number
accepts MutableList<Int>? no yes no
accepts MutableList<Any>? no no yes

The stdlib uses this. Signatures (Kotlin stdlib):

fun <T> MutableCollection<in T>.addAll(elements: Iterable<T>): Boolean
fun <T> Array<out T>.toList(): List<T>
fun <T> MutableList<T>.sortWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>)

addAll accepts a MutableList<Any> as a sink for Iterable<String>. sortWith accepts a Comparator<Any> for a MutableList<String>.

Notes:

  • A projection on a type already declared with the same variance is redundant (warning). One with the opposite variance is an error ("conflicting projection").
  • vararg items: T gives you Array<out T> inside the function. That's why you can pass an Array<String> to a vararg Any via spread.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// A copy helper: source only read, destination only written.
fun <T> copyInto(src: List<T>, dst: MutableList<in T>) {
    src.forEach { dst.add(it) }
}

val ints = listOf(1, 2)
val sink: MutableList<Number> = mutableListOf(3.5)
copyInto(ints, sink)                      // T = Int, dst: MutableList<in Int> accepts MutableList<Number>

fun sumAll(xs: MutableList<out Number>): Double {
    // xs.add(1)                          // error: expected Nothing
    return xs.sumOf { it.toDouble() }
}
sumAll(mutableListOf(1, 2))               // MutableList<Int> accepted

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using MutableList<out T> where List<T> would do. If you only read, take the read-only interface.
  • Expecting get on an in-projected list to return T. It returns Any?, because the list might really be a MutableList<Any>.
  • Forgetting that projections apply per reference. The underlying object is unchanged, so another reference can still mutate it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why doesn't Kotlin need ? extends everywhere like Java? → Declaration-site variance covers the common read-only interfaces once (List, Iterable, Flow<out T>, Sequence<out T>).
  2. What's Array<out Any> useful for? → Functions that read any array, like copy(from: Array<out Any>, to: Array<Any>) in the official docs.
  3. Can you project a type parameter you declared out? → Foo<out T> used as Foo<in X> is a conflicting-projection error. Foo<out X> is redundant.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "use-site is like Java wildcards." The senior answer can predict the projected member signatures (Nothing / Any?), explains why Kotlin needs projections far less, and shows the stdlib's in T sinks and Comparator<in T> patterns.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A generic fun merge(target: MutableList<User>, ...) forced call sites with MutableList<Any> analytics buffers to copy. Changing it to MutableList<in User> removed the copies with zero behavior change.

questions.promptHtml: What does List<*> or MutableList<*> mean? How is it different from List<Any?> and from Java raw types?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Star projections show up in reflection code, when (x) { is List<*> }, and KClass<*>. The question tests whether you know exactly what * projects to for in, out, and invariant parameters.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: * means "some specific type argument I don't know." It's a safe way to refer to any instantiation. For an out parameter, Foo<*> is Foo<out Upper>, so I can read values as the upper bound, usually Any?. For an in parameter it's Foo<in Nothing>, so I can't pass anything in. For an invariant one like MutableList<*>, I can read as Any? but can't add anything. That's different from MutableList<Any?>, which really accepts anything: a MutableList<String> is a MutableList<*> but not a MutableList<Any?>. Unlike Java raw types, star projections are type-safe, and the compiler won't let me write into one.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the official docs:

Declared parameter Foo<*> means You can
Foo<out T : U> Foo<out U> read as U
Foo<in T> Foo<in Nothing> write nothing
Foo<T : U> (invariant) read as Foo<out U>, write as Foo<in Nothing> read as U, write nothing

With several parameters, each is projected independently. For Function1<in P, out R>, Function1<*, String> is Function1<in Nothing, String>: you can't call it with any argument, but you know it returns String.

Comparison:

MutableList<String>  is a  MutableList<*>      YES  (some unknown T)
MutableList<String>  is a  MutableList<Any?>   NO   (invariant)
MutableList<*>       .add(x)                   compile error (in Nothing)
Java raw List        .add(x)                   compiles, heap pollution

Where you'll see it:

  • is List<*> checks, because erasure means the argument can't be checked.
  • KClass<*>, Class<*>, Map<*, *> in reflection, serialization, or DI keys.
  • Heterogeneous containers: Map<KClass<*>, Any>.
  • Java raw types show up in Kotlin as List<*>-like platform types ((Mutable)List<Any?>!).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun printSize(x: Any) {
    if (x is List<*>) {
        val first: Any? = x.firstOrNull()   // reading gives Any?
        println("${x.size} items, first=$first")
    }
}

fun clearAll(lists: List<MutableList<*>>) {
    lists.forEach { it.clear() }            // OK: clear() doesn't mention E
    // lists[0].add("x")                    // error: expected Nothing
}

val registry: Map<KClass<*>, () -> Any> = mapOf(
    String::class to { "" },
    Int::class to { 0 },
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using List<Any?> as a parameter when you mean "any list." It works for List (covariant) but not for MutableList, and the signatures stop matching as soon as someone switches the type.
  • Thinking MutableList<*> is read-only. You can still clear(), removeAt(), and removeAll { }, because those don't take E.
  • Casting list as MutableList<Any?> to add to a star-projected list. That brings back exactly the raw-type unsafety * exists to block.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's Comparable<*>? → Comparable<in Nothing>. You can't call compareTo on it, so it's useless for sorting unless you cast.
  2. What does Function<*, *> let you do? → Nothing, except hold it, compare it, or cast it. Calling requires an in Nothing argument.
  3. When would you prefer a type parameter over *? → When two positions must agree, for example fun <T> swap(list: MutableList<T>, i: Int, j: Int). With * you can't write the element back, even though it came from the same list.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "star means any type, like Java's ?." The senior answer gives the per-variance projection table, the MutableList<*> vs MutableList<Any?> subtyping difference, and the "capture with a type parameter" trick when you need to write back.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Generic RecyclerView or DI registries keyed by KClass<*> are fine. The bug appears when someone casts the value side to a concrete generic type to "make it compile," and that cast is unchecked.

questions.subtopic: Array invariance vs Java covariant arrays
questions.promptHtml: Java arrays are covariant and Kotlin's Array<T> is invariant. Why did Kotlin change this, and what does it mean when you call Java APIs that take arrays?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you understand variance as a soundness issue (Java's ArrayStoreException), plus the practical array details: boxing, vararg, and the fact that arrays are the one place on the JVM where generics are partly reified.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In Java, String[] is an Object[], so you can store an Integer into it through the Object[] reference. The JVM catches that at runtime with an ArrayStoreException. That's a type hole patched with a runtime check. Kotlin makes Array<T> invariant, so Array<String> isn't an Array<Any>, and I use Array<out Any> when I only need to read. Arrays also keep their element class at runtime, unlike List, which is why creating an Array<T> needs a reified T. And Array<Int> is a boxed Integer[], while IntArray is a primitive int[].

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Java:
  Object[] objs = new String[1];   // allowed: covariant arrays
  objs[0] = 42;                    // compiles; runtime ArrayStoreException

Kotlin:
  val objs: Array<Any> = arrayOf<String>("a")       // compile error
  val ro:   Array<out Any> = arrayOf<String>("a")   // OK: read-only projection
  ro[0] = 42                                        // compile error: expected Nothing

Runtime representation:

Kotlin JVM Element class kept?
Array<String> String[] ([Ljava/lang/String;) yes
Array<Int> Integer[] (boxed) yes
IntArray int[] n/a, primitive
Array<List<String>> List[] class only, argument erased

Because arrays know their element class:

  • arrayOf<T>(), arrayOfNulls<T>(), and Array<T>(n) { ... } need a reified T. Otherwise the compiler doesn't know which X[] to allocate.
  • Casting an Object[] to Array<String> is a checked cast at runtime. That's different from List, and it's the source of the generic-array bug in Q153.

Interop:

  • A Java void take(Object[] a) appears in Kotlin as take(a: Array<(out) Any!>!). Kotlin lets you pass Array<String> because Java parameters are treated as flexible out projections.
  • vararg xs: T is Array<out T> inside the function. Passing an existing array needs the spread operator *arr, which copies the array.
  • vararg xs: Int compiles to int... (an IntArray). There's no boxing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun printAll(items: Array<out Any>) = items.forEach(::println)
printAll(arrayOf("a", "b"))                 // OK

fun fill(dest: Array<in String>, v: String) { dest.fill(v) }
val anyArr = arrayOfNulls<Any>(3)
fill(anyArr, "x")                           // OK: Array<Any?> is an Array<in String>

// Boxing difference:
val boxed: Array<Int> = Array(1_000) { it } // 1_000 Integer objects (cached only for -128..127)
val prim: IntArray = IntArray(1_000) { it } // one int[] of 4_000 bytes of payload

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Array<Int> in hot paths (pixel buffers, sensor samples). It's an array of boxed Integer objects. Use IntArray/FloatArray.
  • Writing fun <T> make(n: Int) = arrayOfNulls<T>(n). It doesn't compile without reified, and the common "fix" (arrayOfNulls<Any>(n) as Array<T>) crashes later (Q153).
  • Assuming *arr spread is free. It copies the array on each call.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why didn't Java just make arrays invariant? → Arrays predate generics. Without covariance, Java 1.0 couldn't write Arrays.sort(Object[]) for every array type, so covariance plus a runtime store check was the compromise.
  2. How do you pass a Kotlin Array<String> to a Java method that writes into an Object[]? → It compiles, and Java can still trigger ArrayStoreException. The runtime check is still there.
  3. Is Array<out T> the same as List<T> for reading? → Semantically close, but List has a richer API and no element-class runtime check. Prefer List in Kotlin APIs and keep arrays for interop or primitive performance.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "Kotlin arrays are invariant." The senior answer explains ArrayStoreException as Java's runtime patch, that arrays are the reified exception to erasure (which drives the reified requirement and checked array casts), and the Array<Int> vs IntArray boxing cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom image filter using Array<Float> for a 1080x1920 buffer allocated about 2M boxed objects per frame. Switching to FloatArray removed the GC churn and the jank.

questions.promptHtml: How do reified type parameters work, why do they require inline, and what are their limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Everyone has used inline fun <reified T>. The signal is whether you explain it as compile-time substitution at the call site rather than "Kotlin keeps generic info," and whether you know the edges: nested arguments, Java callers, and calling from non-reified code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A reified type parameter works because the function is inlined. The compiler copies the body into each call site and substitutes the actual type argument, so T::class.java becomes the literal User.class and x is T becomes instanceof User. Nothing survives erasure. The type is known at compile time at every call site. That's why it needs inline: a normal function has one body shared by all callers, so there's nothing to substitute. The limits: the caller must know the concrete type, so a non-reified T can't be forwarded; T::class loses nested arguments, so List<User> becomes just List; Java can't call it; and every call site gets a copy of the body.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
inline fun <reified T : Any> Bundle.parcel(key: String): T? =
    BundleCompat.getParcelable(this, key, T::class.java)

Call site:                         After inlining (conceptually):
val u = args.parcel<User>("u")     val u = BundleCompat.getParcelable(args, "u", User.class)

What reified enables:

  • T::class, T::class.java
  • is T, as T, as? T as real runtime checks (non-reified as T is unchecked and does nothing)
  • arrayOf<T>(), emptyArray<T>()
  • typeOf<T>() (stable since Kotlin 1.6). It keeps nested type arguments and nullability, so typeOf<List<User?>>() is the full KType.

Limits:

  1. No forwarding from non-reified code. fun <T> load() = prefs.read<T>() fails with "Cannot use 'T' as reified type parameter." Every function in the chain must be reified inline, or you must pass a KClass/KType explicitly.
  2. Class-level type parameters can't be reified. Only function type parameters can. For classes, pass KClass<T> or a KType into the constructor.
  3. T::class drops arguments. For T = List<User> you get List::class. Use typeOf<T>() or a TypeToken for full types (Q155).
  4. Java interop. The compiled method exists but isn't usable from Java. A direct call throws UnsupportedOperationException saying the function has a reified type parameter and can only be inlined.
  5. Code size. Each call site gets the inlined body. Keep reified functions tiny, and delegate to a non-inline function that takes Class<T>.
  6. Public inline functions can only touch public (or @PublishedApi internal) API, because their body is compiled into the caller.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Pattern: tiny reified shim -> non-inline worker taking Class<T>
inline fun <reified T : Any> Gson.parse(json: String): T =
    parse(json, object : com.google.gson.reflect.TypeToken<T>() {}.type)

fun <T> Gson.parse(json: String, type: java.lang.reflect.Type): T = fromJson(json, type)

// Broken: forwarding a non-reified T
// fun <T : Any> loadCached(key: String): T = gson.parse(cache[key]!!)   // compile error

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "reified keeps type info at runtime." It doesn't. It's resolved at compile time per call site.
  • Using T::class.java for container types and getting LinkedTreeMap from Gson (Q155).
  • Making large functions inline just to get reified. Split them into a shim and a worker.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does object : TypeToken<T>() {} work inside a reified inline function? → The anonymous class is regenerated per call site with the concrete type in its superclass signature, for example TypeToken<List<User>>, so Gson can read it via getGenericSuperclass().
  2. Can a reified function be called with a type that is itself generic? → Yes, parse<List<User>>(). T::class loses <User>, while typeOf and TypeToken keep it.
  3. How does by viewModels<VM>() use this? → It's an inline reified function that turns VM into VM::class for the ViewModelProvider factory call.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "reified lets you use T::class." The senior answer explains call-site substitution, gives the forwarding and class-parameter limits, separates T::class from typeOf<T>() for nested types, and uses the shim/worker pattern to control code size.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's inline fun <reified T> Api.call() grew to 80 lines, so each of 300 call sites got a full copy. Splitting it into a 2-line reified shim plus a Type-taking worker shrank the dex and kept the ergonomics.

questions.promptHtml: In fun <T> foo(value: T), can value be null? When should you write <T : Any>, and what is T & Any?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It catches people who assume an unbounded T is non-null. This leads to wrong Map/cache semantics, "missing vs null" bugs, and Java interop holes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Yes, it can be null. An unbounded T has the implicit bound Any?, so foo<String?>(null) is legal. Inside, T is "possibly nullable." I can't call members without a safe call, except toString, hashCode, and equals, which have Any? extensions. I write <T : Any> when null must be impossible, for example when the API uses null to mean "absent," or when I need KClass<T>, whose parameter is bounded by Any. T & Any is the definitely non-nullable version of a possibly-nullable T. It's stable since Kotlin 1.7, and it mainly exists for overriding Java methods with @NotNull generic parameters.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
fun <T> f(t: T)          bound Any?   -> T may be String or String?
fun <T : Any> g(t: T)    bound Any    -> T is never nullable
fun <T> h(t: T): T & Any              -> "T, but definitely not null"
fun <T> k(t: T?): T                   -> caller T may still be nullable!

Why it matters:

  1. Absent vs null. Map<K, V>.get(key): V?. If V itself is nullable, null means either "missing" or "present with null." For caches, prefs wrappers, or SavedStateHandle-style stores, bound the value type with V : Any, or return a wrapper/sealed type.
  2. T? doesn't help when T is already nullable. In fun <T> firstOrNullIn(xs: List<T>): T?, if T = String?, then T? is still String?, and a null return is ambiguous again.
  3. APIs that require non-null types. KClass<T : Any>, Class<T> lookups via T::class, java.util.Optional, and lateinit var x: T (lateinit needs a non-null type) all require T : Any.
  4. Java interop. A Java <T> void save(@NotNull T value) implemented in Kotlin needs a parameter type of "T, non-null even if T is nullable." That's T & Any. Without it you'd have to bound the whole class.

T & Any rules: the left side must be a type parameter with a nullable upper bound, and the right side must be exactly Any. Plain Kotlin rarely needs it, because inference handles most cases.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> {                 // V : Any so null always means "absent"
    private val map = HashMap<K, V>()
    operator fun get(key: K): V? = map[key]
    operator fun set(key: K, value: V) { map[key] = value }
}

// Bug-prone version: with T = String?, get() == null is ambiguous
class LooseCache<T> { private val m = HashMap<String, T>(); fun get(k: String): T? = m[k] }

fun <T> T.orThrow(): T & Any = this ?: throw IllegalStateException("null")

val maybe: String? = System.getenv("HOME")
val s: String = maybe.orThrow()               // T = String?, returns String & Any = String

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming fun <T> requireValue(v: T) rejects null. It doesn't. You get T = Nothing? or String? inference.
  • Writing fun <T> ...: T? and believing the return is the only nullable spot. If T is nullable, everything is.
  • Using !! inside generic code to "fix" a nullable T. Bound it instead, so the compiler pushes the decision to callers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does fun <T : Any> f(t: T) compile to for Java? → f(Object) with a @NotNull annotation, plus an Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter call for public functions. Java nulls throw immediately.
  2. Why does fun <T> f(t: T) = t.hashCode() compile? → hashCode() resolves to the Any?.hashCode() extension, which returns 0 for null.
  3. Does <T : Any> change runtime behavior? → Only via the null-check intrinsics on public parameters. Erasure is to Object either way.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "T is non-null unless you write T?." That's wrong. The senior answer knows the Any? default, the absent-vs-null ambiguity, the T?-doesn't-help trap, and when T & Any (1.7+) is needed for Java overrides.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A generic prefs wrapper get<T>(key): T? stored null for "user explicitly cleared." Reads couldn't distinguish that from "never set," so onboarding re-ran for those users. Bounding to T : Any and storing a sentinel fixed the semantics.

questions.subtopic: Nothing as bottom type in generics
questions.promptHtml: How does Nothing work in generics? Why can emptyList() be shared for every element type, and why does UiState.Loading often extend UiState<Nothing>?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It connects the bottom type to covariance, the trick behind clean sealed state hierarchies. Candidates who get this design better Result/UiState types.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Nothing is a subtype of every type, and it has no values. Combine that with covariance: if Foo is declared out T, then Foo<Nothing> is a subtype of Foo<User>, Foo<String>, and every other Foo. So one singleton like the stdlib's internal EmptyList : List<Nothing> can serve as an empty list of anything. The same trick lets object Loading : UiState<Nothing> be a valid UiState<User> without a type parameter on the object, because objects can't have type parameters. It only works with out. For an invariant type, Foo<Nothing> is useless.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Any?
                  |
        Any ... User ... String ...
                  |
               Nothing        (no instances; subtype of all)

With List<out E>:   List<Nothing> <: List<User> <: List<Any>
With MutableList<E>: MutableList<Nothing> unrelated to MutableList<User>

Where Nothing appears:

  • throw, TODO(), error(), and fail() have type Nothing, which is why val x: Int = y ?: error("no y") type-checks.
  • null has type Nothing?, the bottom of the nullable types. listOf(null) infers List<Nothing?>.
  • Stdlib singletons: emptyList(), emptySet(), and emptyMap() return internal objects typed with Nothing, cast to the requested type. Because they're covariant, no element is ever produced, so this is sound.
  • Contravariant positions: Comparable<in Nothing> can't be called, which is exactly what Comparable<*> means.
  • Sealed hierarchies: subclasses that carry no T extend Base<Nothing>.

Why it's sound: a List<Nothing> can never return an element, because there are no Nothing values. Covariance only promises "what you get out is a T," and you never get anything out.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface Load<out T> {
    data object Loading : Load<Nothing>                       // data object: Kotlin 1.9+
    data class Ready<out T>(val value: T) : Load<T>
    data class Failed(val cause: Throwable) : Load<Nothing>
}

fun render(state: Load<List<String>>) = when (state) {
    Load.Loading -> "spinner"
    is Load.Ready -> state.value.joinToString()
    is Load.Failed -> state.cause.message
}

val s: Load<List<String>> = Load.Loading                      // OK: Load<Nothing> <: Load<List<String>>

// Same idea, invariant -> breaks:
sealed interface Bad<T> { object Loading : Bad<Nothing> }
// val b: Bad<String> = Bad.Loading                           // error: type mismatch

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting out on the sealed interface. Then Loading needs Loading<T>() instances, generic classes, and allocations, or unchecked casts.
  • Creating MutableList<Nothing> or MutableStateFlow<Nothing>. Invariant, so useless as a shared "empty."
  • Confusing Nothing (no values) with Unit (exactly one value). List<Unit> can hold items, and List<Nothing> can't.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's the inferred type of listOf(null)? → List<Nothing?>, which widens to any List<X?>.
  2. Why does emptyList<User>() not allocate per call? → It returns the shared EmptyList object. The type argument only exists at compile time.
  3. Can Flow<Nothing> be useful? → Yes. A flow that only completes or fails, for example a "fire this side effect" flow, can be merged into any Flow<T> because Flow is out T.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "Nothing is the type of throw." The senior answer connects bottom type + covariance → shared singletons, explains why it needs out, and uses it to design allocation-free state hierarchies.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A UiState with an invariant T forced Loading<T>() instances and as UiState<User> casts across 40 screens. Adding out and switching to UiState<Nothing> objects deleted every cast.

questions.promptHtml: What does @UnsafeVariance do, when is it legitimate, and which members are exempt from variance checks anyway?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who know variance syntax from people who understand what makes variance sound, which is whether the value is stored or returned.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: @UnsafeVariance suppresses the compiler's variance check for one position. The stdlib uses it on List<out E>.contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E) and indexOf. Those take E as a parameter, which normally breaks out, but they only compare the element and never store it, so no bad value can leak out later. It's legitimate only when the value in the "wrong" position is never stored and never returned as T. Separately, the compiler doesn't check variance on constructor parameters or private members, because outsiders can't use those to inject a wrong value.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The checker is conservative: any parameter of type T in an out T class is an error. Soundness only breaks if an outsider can put a value in that later comes out typed as T.

List<out E>.contains(e: E)     compares, discards       -> safe   -> @UnsafeVariance ok
Cache<out V>.put(v: V)         stores, returned by get  -> unsafe -> @UnsafeVariance is a bug

Exemptions:

  • Constructor parameters (plain parameters, not var properties). The object is being created, and the caller decides T at that moment. class Box<out T>(value: T) is fine, and val properties are output positions anyway.
  • Private members. Variance violations in private declarations aren't reported. Only code inside the class can call them, and the reasoning is "the class author is trusted." That's why class Producer<out T>(private var current: T) compiles. A public var current: T would not.
  • internal/protected are checked. Only private gets the pass.

Heap-pollution demo for the misuse case:

val dogs: Cache<Dog> = Cache()
val animals: Cache<Animal> = dogs     // allowed by out V
animals.put(Cat())                    // allowed by @UnsafeVariance
val d: Dog = dogs.get()               // ClassCastException

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Legit: membership check, no storage.
interface Tags<out T> {
    val all: List<T>
    fun has(tag: @UnsafeVariance T): Boolean = tag in all
}

// Legit: private mutable state in a covariant class.
class Latest<out T>(initial: T) {
    private var value: T = initial                // private: not variance-checked
    fun get(): T = value
    internal fun replaceUnsafe(v: @UnsafeVariance T) { value = v }   // compiles, but THIS is a hole
}

// Correct alternative: split read and write interfaces.
interface Reader<out T> { fun get(): T }
interface Holder<T> : Reader<T> { fun set(v: T) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using @UnsafeVariance to silence an error on a method that stores the value. The compiler was right.
  • Assuming private exemptions extend to internal. They don't, and internal is reachable from the whole module.
  • Exposing a private-backed T setter via a public method. The exemption is about the private member itself. The public method is still where the hole is.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you add a write method to an out interface properly? → Split into Reader<out T> and ReadWrite<T> : Reader<T>, which is the List/MutableList pattern.
  2. Why can Flow<out T> have collect(collector: FlowCollector<T>)? → T inside FlowCollector<in T> in a parameter is two flips, which is an out position. No annotation is needed (Q149).
  3. Is @UnsafeVariance visible to Java? → No. Java sees erased or wildcarded signatures. It's a Kotlin type-checker hint only.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "it turns off the variance error." The senior answer states the soundness criterion (never stored, never returned as T), knows the constructor and private exemptions, and prefers splitting interfaces to annotation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: In a code review, @UnsafeVariance on a covariant event-store append(e) would let a Store<OrderEvent> viewed as Store<Event> accept a LoginEvent. The interface was split into reader and writer instead.

questions.promptHtml: How does Kotlin infer generic type arguments, when does inference fail, and what tools do you have when it does?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Inference failures and surprising inferred types (intersection types, Any, Nothing?) cause confusing compile errors and subtle API types. Seniors should know expected-type flow, builder inference, and _.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin infers type arguments from the value arguments and from the expected type, for example the declared type of the variable or the parameter the result is passed into. When nothing constrains a type variable, as in val x = mutableListOf(), it fails with "Not enough information to infer type variable." When arguments disagree, it picks a common supertype, sometimes an intersection like Comparable<*> & Serializable, which then leaks into my public types. My tools: an explicit type argument (mutableListOf<User>()), a declared variable type, _ to infer just some arguments (stable since Kotlin 1.7), and builder inference for buildList { }-style lambdas. That runs automatically since 1.7, and the K2 compiler in Kotlin 2.0 handles more cases.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Inference collects constraints for each type variable and solves them:

val xs: List<Number> = listOf(1, 2.0)
   constraints on T:  Int <: T, Double <: T, List<T> <: List<Number>
   solution:          T = Number

val ys = listOf(1, "a")
   constraints:       Int <: T, String <: T
   solution:          common supertype = Comparable<*> & java.io.Serializable (an intersection type)

Cases:

  1. Expected type flows inward. val empty: List<User> = emptyList() works, and takeUsers(emptyList()) works.
  2. Return-only type variables can be inferred only from the expected type: fun <T> fromJson(s: String): T works for val u: User = fromJson(s). But fromJson(s).name fails, because there's no expected type.
  3. Lambdas. val f = { x -> x } fails. Write { x: Int -> x } or declare val f: (Int) -> Int.
  4. Builder inference. buildList { add(1) } infers List<Int> from calls inside the lambda. Since Kotlin 1.7 this kicks in automatically when normal inference lacks information, without an annotation. Kotlin 2.0 (K2) improved it further. Verify edge cases against your exact compiler version.
  5. Underscore operator. For fun <S : Settings<T>, T> load(): T, writing load<AppSettings, _>() lets T be inferred from S's bound.
  6. Public API leakage. If a public function's return type is inferred (fun ids() = listOf(1, 2.5)), its signature becomes an intersection type. Explicit API mode (kotlin { explicitApi() }) forces declared return types in libraries.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// val bad = mutableListOf()                  // error: not enough information
val ok = mutableListOf<String>()
val also: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf()

val built = buildList {                       // List<Int>, inferred from add()
    add(1); addAll(listOf(2, 3))
}

abstract class Settings<T> { abstract fun read(): T }
class Flags : Settings<Map<String, Boolean>>() { override fun read() = emptyMap<String, Boolean>() }

inline fun <reified S : Settings<T>, T> load(): T = S::class.java.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance().read()
val flags = load<Flags, _>()                  // T inferred as Map<String, Boolean>

fun mixed() = listOf(1, 2.5)                  // inferred List<{Comparable<*> & Number}>; declare it explicitly
fun mixedFixed(): List<Number> = listOf(1, 2.5)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Letting public APIs infer return types. A later body change silently changes the signature, which breaks binary and source compatibility.
  • Adding casts (as List<Number>) to "help" inference. Use a type argument or an expected type instead. Casts are unchecked.
  • Assuming the inferred type is Any for mixed lists. It's often a narrower intersection type, which surprises people in IDE hints and overload resolution.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does listOf(null) compile? → T is inferred as Nothing?, and List<Nothing?> widens to any List<X?>.
  2. What changed in inference with K2? → The new frontend (FIR) unified the inference pipeline and improved builder inference and smart casts. Check "What's new in Kotlin 2.0" for specifics rather than relying on memory.
  3. When would you use _ instead of a full explicit type? → When one argument is long and derivable, like a generic Map type, but another can't be inferred.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "Kotlin infers types, and you add <T> when it complains." The senior answer explains constraint solving, expected-type inference for return-only type variables, intersection-type leakage into public APIs and explicit API mode, and the version status of builder inference and _.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A library's fun defaults() = mapOf("a" to 1, "b" to 2.0) published Map<String, Comparable<*> & Number>. Tightening it to Map<String, Number> in the next release broke consumers' compiled code. Declaring public return types from day one avoids this.

questions.subtopic: Variance of function types and position flipping
questions.promptHtml: How does variance work for function types? Why can Flow<out T> have a collect(collector: FlowCollector<T>) method even though T appears in a parameter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the deep version of the variance question. It tests whether you can compute variance positions compositionally, which you need to design callback, listener, and Flow-like APIs without sprinkling @UnsafeVariance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A function type (P) -> R is Function1<in P, out R>. It's contravariant in its parameters and covariant in its return. So (Animal) -> String can stand in for (Dog) -> Any. Variance positions compose like signs: an in inside an in becomes an out. In Flow<out T>, collect takes a FlowCollector<T>, and FlowCollector is declared in T. A parameter is an in position, and in T inside it flips again, so T ends up in an out position. That's legal for out T without any annotation. Same reason fun forEach(action: (T) -> Unit) is fine on a covariant type, while fun listener(): (T) -> Unit isn't.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Treat positions as signs: + = out, − = in.

Position                               sign
return type                            +
parameter                              −
type arg of an `out X` type            same as surrounding
type arg of an `in X` type             flipped
type arg of an invariant type          both (+ and −) -> only invariant T allowed

Compose by multiplying:
fun forEach(action: (T) -> Unit)       parameter(−) × Function1.in P(−)   = +   -> OK for out T
fun listener(): (T) -> Unit            return(+)    × Function1.in P(−)   = −   -> ERROR for out T
fun map(f: (T) -> R): Box<R>           parameter(−) × in P(−)             = +   -> OK
suspend fun collect(c: FlowCollector<T>)  parameter(−) × in T(−)          = +   -> OK
fun sink(): MutableList<T>             return(+) × invariant              = ±   -> ERROR for out T

Intuition for the flip: in forEach(action), the box calls the action and gives it a T. Values of T flow out of the box into the callback, so the box is producing T even though T appears in a parameter list.

Subtyping of function types:

(Animal) -> Dog  <:  (Dog) -> Animal
   accepts more (param contravariant), returns less (return covariant)

Design consequences:

  • Callback interfaces should be fun interface Listener<in T> { fun onEvent(e: T) }. Then one Listener<Any> (a logger) can register on every EventSource<Order>.
  • Producer types taking callbacks (subscribe(listener: Listener<T>)) can be out T, which mirrors Flow.
  • If a method returns a callback that accepts T, the type must be invariant or in.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun interface Listener<in T> { fun onEvent(event: T) }

interface EventSource<out T> {
    fun subscribe(listener: Listener<T>)      // − × − = +  : fine for out T
    // fun currentListener(): Listener<T>     // + × − = −  : error for out T
}

open class Event
class OrderPlaced : Event()

fun wire(orders: EventSource<OrderPlaced>, all: EventSource<Event>) {
    val logAll = Listener<Any> { println(it) }
    orders.subscribe(logAll)                  // Listener<Any> <: Listener<OrderPlaced>
    all.subscribe(logAll)

    val generic: (Event) -> String = { it.toString() }
    val handler: (OrderPlaced) -> Any = generic   // (Event)->String <: (OrderPlaced)->Any
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring callback interfaces invariant by default (Callback<T>). Every caller then needs an exact-type callback, and generic loggers or analytics sinks can't be shared.
  • Thinking a parameter is always an in position. It's only in at the first level. Nested function types flip it.
  • Adding @UnsafeVariance where position math shows the code is already legal, or where it shows a real hole.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is suspend (T) -> Unit variant the same way? → Yes. Suspend function types have the same variance in their parameters and return, with an extra continuation added in the JVM signature.
  2. What about T.() -> Unit (receiver)? → The receiver is a parameter, so it's in (contravariant), just like a normal first parameter.
  3. Why is StateFlow<out T> covariant but MutableStateFlow<T> invariant? → MutableStateFlow adds var value: T and emit(T), which are in positions at the first level, so it must be invariant. Read-only exposure (asStateFlow()) gives callers covariance.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "function types are in for params and out for return." The senior answer computes nested positions as sign multiplication, explains Flow.collect and forEach with it, and designs listener APIs with in T so they compose.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK's Callback<T> was invariant, so apps wrote one adapter class per event type just to forward to a common logger. Releasing Callback<in T> (source-compatible for Kotlin callers) removed dozens of adapters.

questions.subtopic: Generic info that survives erasure (super type tokens, typeOf)
questions.promptHtml: If generics are erased, how do Gson, Retrofit, Moshi, and kotlinx.serialization know that a field or return type is List<User>? What are super type tokens and typeOf<T>()?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors are expected to know exactly what erasure removes. That knowledge is what lets you debug serialization and R8 issues instead of cargo-culting keep rules.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Erasure removes type arguments from values and expressions, but the compiler still writes generic declaration signatures into the class file as Signature attributes. That covers fields, method parameters and returns, and superclasses. Reflection exposes them through Field.genericType, Method.genericReturnType, and Class.genericSuperclass. Retrofit reads the generic return type of your interface method, and that's how it knows List<User>. A super type token exploits the superclass case: object : TypeToken<List<User>>() {} creates an anonymous subclass whose superclass signature records List<User>. In Kotlin, typeOf<T>() with a reified T gives a full KType, including nested arguments and nullability, computed at the call site. Strip the Signature attributes with R8, and every reflection-based approach breaks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kept in class file:
  class UserList : ArrayList<User>()          Signature: Ljava/util/ArrayList<Lcom/app/User;>;
  val users: List<User>                       field Signature: Ljava/util/List<Lcom/app/User;>;
  suspend fun users(): List<User>             method Signature (return is erased into the
                                              Continuation<? super List<User>> parameter)
Not kept:
  val local = listOf<User>()                  local variable type args (no runtime record)
  fun <T> f() { ... T ... }                   T inside the body is just its bound

Three ways to get a full type at runtime:

Technique How Needs
Declared signature Method.getGenericReturnType(), Field.getGenericType() -keepattributes Signature in R8
Super type token object : TypeToken<List<User>>() {}.type reads getGenericSuperclass() Signature kept on the anonymous class
typeOf<T>() Compiler builds a KType at the reified call site Kotlin 1.6+ (stable). No reflection lookup for the type itself
Codegen kotlinx.serialization plugin or Moshi codegen generate serializers at compile time No runtime type discovery needed

Retrofit and suspend: for suspend fun users(): List<User>, the JVM method's return is Object, and the real type lives in the last parameter Continuation<? super List<User>>. Retrofit reads that parameter's generic type. That's why R8 rules for Retrofit + coroutines must keep kotlin.coroutines.Continuation signatures.

typeOf<T>() notes:

  • Works with nullability: typeOf<List<String?>>() differs from typeOf<List<String>>().
  • The classifier and arguments are available without the full kotlin-reflect artifact. Deeper reflection (members, annotations) needs kotlin-reflect.
  • Converting to a Java Type uses KType.javaType. Check whether it requires an opt-in in your Kotlin version before relying on it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType
import kotlin.reflect.typeOf

// Hand-rolled super type token:
abstract class TypeRef<T> {
    val type: java.lang.reflect.Type =
        (javaClass.genericSuperclass as ParameterizedType).actualTypeArguments[0]
}
val usersType = object : TypeRef<List<User>>() {}.type   // java.util.List<com.app.User>

// Kotlin-native:
inline fun <reified T> describe(): String = typeOf<T>().toString()
// describe<Map<String, List<Int?>>>() -> "kotlin.collections.Map<kotlin.String, kotlin.collections.List<kotlin.Int?>>"

// Broken: a non-reified generic captures a type *variable*, not a type
fun <T> brokenRef(): java.lang.reflect.Type = object : TypeRef<List<T>>() {}.type   // java.util.List<T>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Creating the TypeToken inside a non-reified generic function. You get List<T> with T as a TypeVariable, and Gson treats elements as Object, which means LinkedTreeMap (Q155).
  • Assuming debug behavior equals release. R8 full mode strips Signature attributes from classes not matched by keep rules (Q156).
  • Using T::class when you need typeOf<T>(). Only the latter keeps nested arguments.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the TypeRef class have to be abstract or anonymous-subclassed? → The type argument is only recorded in a subclass's superclass signature. TypeRef<List<User>>() without a subclass records nothing.
  2. Why do codegen serializers avoid this whole class of bugs? → The serializer for List<User> is resolved at compile time (for example kotlinx.serialization's serializer<List<User>>()), so nothing depends on runtime signatures.
  3. Does typeOf work for a class-level T? → No. It needs a reified function type parameter. Pass a KType into the class constructor from a reified factory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "use TypeToken for lists." The senior answer explains why it works (Signature attributes on the anonymous subclass), how Retrofit finds suspend return types through Continuation, why the token must be built with concrete types, and that R8 and codegen are what decide release-time robustness.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that understand "reflection reads Signature attributes" fix release-only Gson and Retrofit crashes in minutes. Teams that don't add -keep class ** { *; } and lose most of R8's size savings.

questions.promptHtml: What does T : Comparable<T> mean, and how do you write a fluent builder hierarchy in Kotlin, which has no self type?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Recursive generics appear in Enum<E : Enum<E>>, Comparable, and builder APIs. It tests advanced bound reasoning and whether you know idiomatic Kotlin alternatives to Java's "curiously recurring template pattern."

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: T : Comparable<T> is a recursive bound. It means "a T that can be compared with other Ts," which is what sorted() and maxOf need. For builders, Java uses Builder<B extends Builder<B>> so base-class setters return the subclass type. Kotlin has no Self type, so the same pattern needs an abstract self() or an unchecked this as B. In Kotlin I usually skip it altogether: named and default arguments, copy() on data classes, or apply {} on the concrete type give fluent construction. If I really need base methods that return the caller's type, a generic extension fun <T : Base> T.withX(): T = apply { ... } does it without recursive generics.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Recursive bounds in the stdlib and JDK:

interface Comparable<in T>        -> fun <T : Comparable<T>> Iterable<T>.sorted(): List<T>
abstract class Enum<E : Enum<E>>  -> lets Enum.compareTo(other: E) take only the same enum type

Why T : Comparable<T> and not T : Comparable<Any>: Int implements Comparable<Int>, not Comparable<Any>. The recursive bound says "comparable to its own kind." Thanks to Comparable<in T>, a subclass that inherits Comparable<Base> also satisfies a Comparable<Sub>-style requirement, because contravariance makes Comparable<Base> a Comparable<Sub>.

Builder hierarchy, the Java-style way:

abstract class RequestBuilder<B : RequestBuilder<B>> {
    fun header(k, v): B { ...; return self() }   // returns the concrete subtype
    protected abstract fun self(): B
}
class ImageRequestBuilder : RequestBuilder<ImageRequestBuilder>() { override fun self() = this }

Costs:

  • Every reference becomes RequestBuilder<*>, or you have to repeat the self parameter.
  • Nothing stops class Evil : RequestBuilder<ImageRequestBuilder>(). The bound can't enforce "B is exactly me."
  • Java callers see the same verbosity.

Kotlin alternatives:

Need Idiom
Configure many optional fields constructor with defaults + named args
Modified copy of immutable config data class + copy(...)
Fluent mutation on any subclass fun <T : Base> T.tag(t: String): T = apply { tags += t }
DSL-style construction lambdas with receiver (see the DSL chunk)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun <T : Comparable<T>> List<T>.isSortedAsc(): Boolean = zipWithNext().all { (a, b) -> a <= b }

open class Request { val headers = mutableMapOf<String, String>() }
class ImageRequest : Request() { var sizePx: Int = 0 }

// Self-type-free fluent API: the extension returns the receiver's static type.
fun <T : Request> T.header(k: String, v: String): T = apply { headers[k] = v }

val req: ImageRequest = ImageRequest()
    .header("Accept", "image/webp")       // still ImageRequest
    .apply { sizePx = 512 }

// Java-style recursive builder, if you must interoperate:
abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> {
    protected val headers = mutableMapOf<String, String>()
    protected abstract fun self(): B
    fun header(k: String, v: String): B { headers[k] = v; return self() }
}
class ImageBuilder : Builder<ImageBuilder>() {
    override fun self() = this
    fun size(px: Int) = apply { /* ... */ }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") return this as B instead of an abstract self(). It works until someone declares a mismatched subclass.
  • Porting Java builders 1:1 to Kotlin. Default arguments make most builders unnecessary, except for Java consumers.
  • Writing fun <T : Comparable<Any>> and wondering why listOf(1, 2).isSorted() doesn't compile.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Enum declared Enum<E : Enum<E>>? → So compareTo and EnumSet-style APIs accept only constants of the same enum type.
  2. Would Kotlin's Self type proposals change this? → There have been design discussions about self types, but nothing is stable as of Kotlin 2.x as far as I know. Don't design around it.
  3. Does the extension approach work from Java? → It's a static method header(Request, k, v) returning Request erased to the bound, so Java loses the fluent subtype. Use the recursive builder only if Java ergonomics matter.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer can read T : Comparable<T>. The senior answer explains why it's recursive (Int is Comparable<Int>), how in T makes subclass comparables fit, the limits of the recursive builder pattern, and the idiomatic Kotlin replacements.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A networking SDK's 3-level Builder<B : Builder<B>> hierarchy produced unreadable inference errors for app teams. Replacing it with a data-class config plus copy() cut the public API surface roughly in half with no loss of features.

questions.contextHtml:
A shared in-memory cache is used by 12 feature modules. Crashlytics shows a new crash on the Profile screen: 0.4% of sessions, starting with the release that added "prefetch profile on login" in a different module. Nobody touched the Profile screen.

object MemoryCache {
    private val map = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, Any>()
    fun put(key: String, value: Any) { map[key] = value }

    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    fun <T> get(key: String): T? = map[key] as? T        // "safe cast, returns null if wrong type"
}

// Login module (new):
MemoryCache.put("profile", profileDtoFromLogin)          // ProfileDto

// Profile module (old):
val user: User? = MemoryCache.get("profile")             // ProfileViewModel.kt:42
user?.let { render(it) } ?: loadFromNetwork()
Fatal Exception: java.lang.ClassCastException: com.app.login.ProfileDto cannot be cast to com.app.profile.User
    at com.app.profile.ProfileViewModel.load(ProfileViewModel.kt:42)

The release also bumped Room and enabled a new R8 rule. Those are red herrings.
questions.promptHtml: What's the bug, why does the "safe cast" not return null, and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in try/catch," or "rename the key." Both treat the symptom. They don't explain why as? T didn't return null, so the same pattern stays in the other 11 modules.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who else writes "profile"? (Key collisions across modules.) How many get<T> call sites exist? (Blast radius.) Is the cache process-wide? (Yes, object.) Is the crash only on fresh logins? (That would match the new prefetch.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the Profile call site to MemoryCache.get<Any>("profile") as? User, which is a real checked cast, or rename the login key. Ship it behind the normal hotfix process. No server change is needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) A key collision plus an unchecked generic cast. This fits the stack: the crash is at the caller line, not inside the cache.
    • (b) R8 merged or renamed classes so ProfileDto and User got confused. Unlikely: the message names two distinct real classes.
    • (c) A Room migration returning the wrong entity. It's in the release notes, but the stack shows no Room frames.
  4. How I'd verify each: Grep for put("profile" across modules. Write a unit test: put("k", "string"); val x: Int? = get("k"), which reproduces a ClassCastException on the JVM without Android. Check the decompiled bytecode of get. There's no instanceof and no checkcast inside it, and the checkcast User is in ProfileViewModel.load.
  5. Root cause: T is erased to Any? inside get, so map[key] as? T compiles to "cast to Object," which always succeeds. The compiler warned ("Unchecked cast"), and the @Suppress hid it. The real checkcast User is inserted at the call site where the result is assigned to User?, and that throws. So as? never had a chance to return null, and the crash shows up in the module that didn't change.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: make get reified so the check is real.
    • Long-term: typed keys. Each key carries its type, so a collision becomes a compile-time or registration error.
    object MemoryCache {
    private val map = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<Key<*>, Any>()

    class Key<T : Any>(val name: String, val type: kotlin.reflect.KClass<T>)

    fun <T : Any> put(key: Key<T>, value: T) { map[key] = value }
    fun <T : Any> get(key: Key<T>): T? = key.type.safeCast(map[key])   // real runtime check
}
// Keys are declared once, per module, and are distinct objects even with equal names:
val ProfileUserKey = MemoryCache.Key("profile", User::class)

// Minimal short-term fix if the API must stay string-keyed:
inline fun <reified T> getChecked(key: String): T? = rawGet(key) as? T   // reified: real instanceof
  7. Prevention: A Detekt/lint rule or review checklist item: no @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") on as T/as? T without a comment justifying why it's safe. Treat the compiler's unchecked-cast warning as an error in shared modules (allWarningsAsErrors per module, if the team can sustain it). Add a contract test for the cache with mismatched types.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't catch ClassCastException around every get. It hides real bugs and costs a stack-trace fill each time. I wouldn't key by KClass alone either, because two features may legitimately cache two different Users. Typed keys give both identity and type.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if T is List<User>? → Even reified as? T only checks List. Use a key carrying a KType (typeOf<List<User>>()), or wrap it in a dedicated class like UserList(val items: List<User>).
  • Why didn't the unit tests in Profile catch it? → They used a fake cache, or only put Users. The bug needs two modules sharing global state, so it needs a cross-module integration test or typed keys.
  • Is ConcurrentHashMap relevant? → No. Thread safety is fine here. It's a type-safety bug.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite but typical case: a "generic" SharedPrefs.get<T>(key) with as T survived two years until a migration stored an Int where a Long had been. Crashes appeared on app start for upgraded users only. Typed keys turned the next attempt into a compile error.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests try/catch or key renaming without explaining why as? T doesn't work.
  • Hire: Explains erasure makes as? T unchecked, that the checkcast is at the call site, and fixes it with reified.
