  • Strong hire: Also designs typed keys, handles the nested-generic KType case, and adds the lint/warning policy so the other 11 modules are covered.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate wrote a fixed-size ring buffer for recent search queries. Unit tests with RingBuffer<Int> pass. In the app, the search screen crashes on open for every user who has search history. That's 100% repro on the internal dogfood build.

class RingBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) {
    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    private val items: Array<T?> = arrayOfNulls<Any?>(capacity) as Array<T?>
    private var head = 0
    private var size = 0

    fun add(item: T) { items[(head + size) % capacity] = item; if (size < capacity) size++ else head = (head + 1) % capacity }

    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    fun snapshot(): Array<T> = Array<Any?>(size) { items[(head + it) % capacity] } as Array<T>
}

// SearchViewModel
private val recent = RingBuffer<String>(20)
val chips: Array<String> = recent.snapshot()          // SearchViewModel.kt:31
java.lang.ClassCastException: java.lang.Object[] cannot be cast to java.lang.String[]
    at com.app.search.SearchViewModel.<init>(SearchViewModel.kt:31)

Red herrings: the crash started after the Compose BOM update, and the tests use RingBuffer<Int> but only call add/size.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the crash, why the tests didn't catch it, and fix the class.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Array<String> directly," or "add @Suppress." Or blaming Compose. Weak answers don't recognize that arrays carry their element class at runtime while the generic T is erased.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does anything need a real Array, or would a List do? (Usually a list.) Is this used with primitives in hot paths? (That would mean a separate IntArray-backed class.) Which call sites call snapshot()?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Change the one call site to recent.snapshot().toList(). That still crashes, because the checkcast String[] happens at the assignment. So the real hotfix is changing snapshot()'s return type to List<T>. It's a one-file change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The unchecked array cast escapes the class. That matches the message exactly: Object[] → String[]. (b) Compose BOM. No Compose frames in the stack, so no. (c) Data corruption in persisted history. Then the message would mention element types, not array types.
  4. How I'd verify each: A JVM unit test val a: Array<String> = RingBuffer<String>(2).apply { add("x") }.snapshot() reproduces it instantly. Decompiled bytecode shows snapshot() returns Object[] and the caller does CHECKCAST [Ljava/lang/String;.
  5. Root cause: Inside the class, T is erased, so Array<T> is really Object[]. That's fine as long as the array never leaves the class, which is exactly how java.util.ArrayList stores elements. snapshot() returns the Object[] typed as Array<T>. At the call site T = String, so the compiler inserts checkcast String[]. Unlike List, arrays carry their element class at runtime, so this cast is checked and fails. The tests used Int but never assigned snapshot() to an Array<Int>, so no checkcast was ever executed.
  6. Fix: 
    class RingBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) {
    private val items = arrayOfNulls<Any?>(capacity)       // honest internal type
    private var head = 0
    private var size = 0

    fun add(item: T) {
        items[(head + size) % capacity] = item
        if (size < capacity) size++ else head = (head + 1) % capacity
    }

    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")                             // safe: only T is ever stored
    fun snapshot(): List<T> = List(size) { items[(head + it) % capacity] as T }
}

// If callers truly need an array, make the caller's type concrete:
inline fun <reified T> RingBuffer<T>.snapshotArray(): Array<T> = snapshot().toTypedArray()
    toTypedArray() is itself reified, so it allocates a real String[].
  7. Prevention: A review rule that a generic class never returns an Array<T> built from Object[]. Tests for generic containers must exercise every public method with a non-Any type argument and assign results to concrete types. A Detekt rule that flags as Array< casts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't require a Class<T> constructor parameter just to allocate java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance. That's valid but adds ceremony for a 20-item list. I'd also avoid ArrayDeque only if we needed a fixed capacity. Otherwise ArrayDeque<T> from the stdlib already solves this, and I'd delete the custom class.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does Java's ArrayList.toArray() return Object[]? → Same reason: it can't know T. That's why toArray(T[] a) takes an array to learn the element class.
  • Would the reified extension work from a non-reified generic caller? → No. The caller must know the concrete type (Q144).
  • Does the internal Object[] cost anything vs String[]? → No meaningful difference. The cost is boxing if T is a primitive like Int.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A generic "matrix" utility returned Array<Array<T>> built from Object[][] and was only ever used with Any in tests. The first real Array<Array<Float>> caller crashed in production. The fix was returning List<List<T>> and adding a specialized FloatArray version for the hot path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames Compose, or suggests more suppression.
  • Hire: Explains erased T vs reified array element class and the call-site checkcast. Returns List<T>.
  • Strong hire: Also explains why the tests missed it, offers the reified toTypedArray() option, and points out that the stdlib ArrayDeque already covers most needs.

questions.contextHtml:
You're reviewing a PR in a core-users module used by 9 feature modules. Since it landed, three teams have added copy-paste comparators and one added an unchecked cast. Code under review:

open class User(val id: String, val lastSeen: Long)
class Admin(id: String, lastSeen: Long, val permissions: Set<String>) : User(id, lastSeen)
class Guest(id: String) : User(id, 0)

val byLastSeen: Comparator<User> = compareByDescending { it.lastSeen }

fun <T> MutableList<T>.sortSafely(cmp: Comparator<T>) { sortWith(cmp) }
fun mergeInto(target: MutableList<User>, src: List<User>) { target.addAll(src) }
fun countActive(users: MutableList<User>): Int = users.count { it.lastSeen > 0 }

// Feature module A:
val admins: MutableList<Admin> = loadAdmins()
admins.sortSafely(byLastSeen)                                  // doesn't compile -> they wrote byLastSeenAdmin
@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
mergeInto(admins as MutableList<User>, listOf(Guest("g1")))    // compiles
admins.first().permissions                                     // Crashlytics: Guest cannot be cast to Admin
questions.promptHtml: What would you change in the API and why? Explain the crash.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make everything MutableList<Any>," or "write overloads for Admin." Both increase the surface without addressing the invariant signatures that forced the casts.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do callers ever need to mutate in countActive? (No. It reads.) Should mergeInto be allowed to put Guests into an Admin list at all? (No, and that's the real bug.) Are there Java callers? (That affects wildcard visibility, but not the fix.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the unchecked cast in module A. Merge Guests into a separate MutableList<User>, or filter. It crashes today for users whose admin list gets a guest merged in.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: There's only one real cause, invariant signatures plus an escape-hatch cast. The things to check are where else the same cast pattern exists (grep for as MutableList<), and whether any other comparator duplicates diverged in behavior (the copies might sort differently).
  4. How I'd verify each: Grep plus a compile check after changing signatures. Every copy-paste comparator should become deletable. Unit test: mutableListOf<Admin>().sortSafely(byLastSeen) compiles.
  5. Root cause: sortSafely takes Comparator<T>, and Comparator (java.util.Comparator) is invariant in Kotlin's view. With T = Admin, a Comparator<User> isn't accepted, even though a comparator of Users can obviously compare Admins. mergeInto takes MutableList<User>, which is invariant, so an Admin list can't be passed. The team cast it, and the cast is unchecked due to erasure. addAll then put a Guest into the admins list, and the checkcast Admin at first() failed.
  6. Fix: 
    fun <T> MutableList<T>.sortSafely(cmp: Comparator<in T>) { sortWith(cmp) }   // consumer -> in
fun mergeInto(target: MutableList<in User>, src: Iterable<User>) { target.addAll(src) }
fun countActive(users: Iterable<User>): Int = users.count { it.lastSeen > 0 } // read-only -> covariant

admins.sortSafely(byLastSeen)              // OK now: Comparator<User> is a Comparator<in Admin>
// mergeInto(admins, listOf(Guest("g1")))  // still (correctly) rejected: MutableList<Admin> is not MutableList<in User>
    Now the compiler accepts every safe call and rejects exactly the bug.
  7. Prevention: A review checklist for shared modules: parameters that only read take Iterable/List/out, sinks take in, comparators and callbacks take in T. Make the unchecked-cast warning an error in feature modules. Delete the duplicated comparators.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't widen to MutableList<Any> or MutableList<*>. It loses type information and pushes casts to callers. I wouldn't add Admin-specific overloads, which scale linearly with subclasses. Changing parameter types from MutableList<User> to Iterable<User> is source-compatible for Kotlin callers. For Java callers or already-compiled consumers, the erased descriptor changes (List → Iterable), so for a published library I'd add the new overloads and deprecate the old ones.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does the stdlib sortWith already take Comparator<in T>? → Exactly this reason. The wrapper's invariant signature threw away what the stdlib gave.
  • Is Comparator declared in in Kotlin? → On the JVM, kotlin.Comparator is a typealias to java.util.Comparator, which Kotlin sees as invariant. That's why use-site in is required.
  • Could mergeInto be generic instead? → fun <T> mergeInto(target: MutableList<in T>, src: Iterable<T>) works too. The compiler infers T and still rejects Guests into Admins.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "utils" module with invariant MutableList<T> parameters everywhere was the source of most unchecked casts in a 30-module app. A one-day variance pass on its 40 public functions removed about 25 casts and two duplicate comparator implementations that had drifted apart.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Doesn't see the unchecked cast as the crash cause, or proposes Any.
  • Hire: Applies Comparator<in T>, MutableList<in User>, and read-only Iterable, and explains the crash via erasure.
  • Strong hire: Also notes the compiler still correctly rejects the Guest merge, covers binary compatibility for published modules, and adds a review checklist for shared APIs.

questions.contextHtml:
E-commerce app, 2.1M DAU. A refactor "extracted a generic JSON helper" to replace 60 hand-written TypeTokens. After rollout to 50%, the crash-free sessions rate drops from 99.85% to 98.3%, all on the Orders and Wishlist screens. Product screens work fine.

inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJsonTyped(json: String): T = fromJson(json, T::class.java)

// OrdersRepository
val orders: List<Order> = gson.fromJsonTyped(body)
// ProductRepository
val product: Product = gson.fromJsonTyped(body)
Fatal Exception: java.lang.ClassCastException: com.google.gson.internal.LinkedTreeMap cannot be cast to com.app.orders.Order
    at com.app.orders.OrdersViewModel$uiState$1.invokeSuspend(OrdersViewModel.kt:57)

Same day, the backend changed the createdAt date format, and Gson was bumped by a minor version. Those are red herrings, but the on-call engineer suspects both.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosing and fixing this.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Backend changed the date format, so roll back the backend," or "add @SerializedName." Neither explains LinkedTreeMap, and neither explains why Product works and List<Order> doesn't.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which screens crash: only ones parsing collections or generic wrappers? (Yes: Orders = List<Order>, Wishlist = Page<Item>.) Does the crash happen at parse time or later? (Later. The stack is in the ViewModel, not Gson.) Are debug builds affected? (Yes, so it's not R8.) When did the helper ship relative to the backend change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout at 50% in Play Console. Remote-config the Orders and Wishlist screens back to the old parsing path if one exists. Otherwise prepare a hotfix release, since there's nothing server-side to roll back that would help.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) The helper passes a raw Class for generic types. LinkedTreeMap is Gson's representation of a JSON object when it doesn't know the target type. That points straight at lost type arguments.
    • (b) The Gson version bump changed collection handling. Possible, but it wouldn't explain the Product/Orders split.
    • (c) The date format change. That would throw JsonSyntaxException or produce wrong dates, not a ClassCastException on the element type.
  4. How I'd verify each: A JVM unit test: gson.fromJsonTyped<List<Order>>("""[{"id":"1"}]""").first() throws the same exception, and Product parses. Logging T::class.java inside the helper prints interface java.util.List. Bisect by reverting the helper on one screen.
  5. Root cause: With T = List<Order>, T::class.java is java.util.List.class. Reified keeps the class, but nested arguments are dropped. Gson is told "parse a List of unknown elements," so it builds an ArrayList<LinkedTreeMap>. Erasure lets that object be returned as List<Order> without any check. The crash only happens when a compiler-inserted checkcast Order runs on element access in the ViewModel. Product works because a plain class has no type arguments to lose.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: build a full Type from the reified parameter. 
      import com.google.gson.reflect.TypeToken

inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJsonTyped(json: String): T =
    fromJson(json, object : TypeToken<T>() {}.type)   // anonymous class per call site records List<Order>
      Alternatives: TypeToken.getParameterized(List::class.java, Order::class.java).type, or a typeOf<T>()-based conversion (check javaType opt-in status for your Kotlin version).
    • Long-term: move to a codegen serializer (kotlinx.serialization or Moshi with codegen). Types are resolved at compile time, Kotlin nullability and defaults are honored (Gson ignores both, see the null-safety chunk), and R8 needs no Signature-preservation rules.
  7. Prevention:
    • A parameterized unit test per generic shape (List<X>, Map<String, X>, Page<X>), asserting element types with assertIs<Order>(list.first()), not just list size.
    • Lint or code review: ban T::class.java passed to fromJson.
    • Watch the crash-free rate by screen in the staged rollout, with automatic halt thresholds.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't roll back the backend. It costs another team a deploy and doesn't touch the cause. I wouldn't revert to 60 hand-written TypeTokens. The reified TypeToken helper is correct and keeps the DRY win. And I wouldn't add -keep rules: this crashes in debug too, so it isn't a shrinker problem (contrast with Q156).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would fun <T> Gson.fromJsonTyped(json: String): T = fromJson(json, object : TypeToken<T>() {}.type) without reified work? → No. The token records the type variable T. Recent Gson versions reject TypeTokens that capture a type variable with an explicit error, as I recall. Older ones silently produced LinkedTreeMap. Either way, reified is needed.
  • Why does the crash show in a coroutine frame, not in the repository? → The repository returned the polluted list as-is. The first element access is inside the uiState flow's mapping lambda in the ViewModel.
  • How many bytes does the per-call-site anonymous class cost? → One small class per call site. With 60 call sites it's negligible, but it's the reason to keep the inline function tiny.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a "cleanup" PR consolidated parsing helpers on a Friday, and the date-format change on the same day sent the team chasing the backend for hours. The LinkedTreeMap in the message was the clue they should have trusted first, since it always means Gson didn't know the element type.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Chases the date format or the Gson version without connecting LinkedTreeMap to lost type arguments.
  • Hire: Identifies T::class.java dropping nested arguments, and fixes it with a reified TypeToken or getParameterized.
  • Strong hire: Explains why the crash is deferred (erasure plus checkcast), rules out R8 using the debug repro, proposes codegen serializers long-term, and adds shape-based tests and rollout guardrails.

questions.contextHtml:
You upgrade AGP from 7.4 to 8.x and Kotlin to 2.0 in one PR. Debug builds and all unit tests pass. The internal release build (minified) crashes on the first network call on all devices:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: TypeToken must be created with a type argument: new TypeToken<...>() {};
  When using code shrinkers (ProGuard, R8, ...) make sure that generic signatures are preserved.
    at com.google.gson.reflect.TypeToken.<init>(...)
    at com.app.data.CartRepository$special$$inlined$fromJsonTyped$1.<init>(...)
java.lang.ClassCastException: java.lang.Class cannot be cast to java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType
    at retrofit2.HttpServiceMethod.parseAnnotations(...)

Gson is 2.10.1, and Retrofit is pinned to an older 2.x. The release goes to 8M users in 10 days. A teammate proposes reverting the Kotlin 2.0 upgrade, "because K2 changed how reified works."
questions.promptHtml: What happened, and how do you get the upgrade out safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Revert to Kotlin 1.9," or "add -keep class ** { *; }." The first misattributes the cause. The second kills shrinking and obfuscation for the whole app, and can add many MB to the APK.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does android.enableR8.fullMode appear in gradle.properties? (AGP 8.0 made full mode the default.) Is the crash reproducible with Kotlin 1.9 + AGP 8? (That isolates the cause.) Which Gson and Retrofit versions, since newer ones ship consumer keep rules? Do we have a minified build in CI at all?
  2. Immediate mitigation: This isn't in production yet, so nothing is bleeding. As a time-boxed unblock I can set android.enableR8.fullMode=false to get back to the old R8 behavior while I fix the rules properly. I'd only ship with that if the deadline forces it, with a tracked follow-up.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) R8 full mode strips Signature attributes from classes not matched by keep rules. The Gson message literally says so, and Retrofit's Class cannot be cast to ParameterizedType means it found a raw return type where a generic one was expected.
    • (b) K2 changed reified codegen. Testable quickly. Unlikely, since debug works on the same compiler.
    • (c) An AGP 8 namespace or BuildConfig change. That causes different failures (build errors or missing constants), not reflection crashes.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Build release with full mode on and off. The crash disappears with it off.
    • Use -printconfiguration to see the merged rules, and check whether -keepattributes Signature and the TypeToken rules are present.
    • Inspect the release APK in Android Studio's APK Analyzer (Show Bytecode) on the anonymous fromJsonTyped$1 class. The superclass Signature attribute is gone.
    • Kotlin 1.9 + AGP 8 also crashes, which rules out K2.
  5. Root cause: Gson's TypeToken and Retrofit both recover generic types at runtime by reading Signature attributes (Q150). In R8 full mode, those attributes are kept only for classes, methods, and fields matched by keep rules. The anonymous TypeToken subclasses and the Retrofit service methods weren't matched, so getGenericSuperclass() returned a raw Class and getGenericReturnType() lost List<CartItem>. Debug builds don't run R8, so everything worked there.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term (rules), if libraries can't be upgraded yet: 
      -keepattributes Signature, InnerClasses, EnclosingMethod
-keepattributes RuntimeVisibleAnnotations, RuntimeVisibleParameterAnnotations, AnnotationDefault

# Gson TypeToken and its anonymous subclasses
-keep class com.google.gson.reflect.TypeToken { *; }
-keep class * extends com.google.gson.reflect.TypeToken

# Retrofit service interfaces + suspend return types
-keep,allowobfuscation,allowshrinking interface retrofit2.Call
-keep,allowobfuscation,allowshrinking class retrofit2.Response
-keep,allowobfuscation,allowshrinking class kotlin.coroutines.Continuation
-if interface * { @retrofit2.http.* <methods>; }
-keep,allowobfuscation interface <1>
    • Long-term: upgrade Gson to 2.11+, which bundles its full-mode keep rules, and Retrofit to a version that ships full-mode rules (check its changelog). Then delete the hand-written copies. Also keep model fields: Gson's field reflection needs @SerializedName or keep rules on models, and full mode no longer implicitly keeps no-arg constructors. Better still, migrate models to a codegen serializer so none of this applies.
    • Don't revert Kotlin 2.0. It isn't the cause.
  7. Prevention:
    • CI builds and smoke-tests a minified variant: an instrumented test of the top 5 API calls on a benchmark/minifiedDebug build type with R8 enabled.
    • Separate risky upgrades: AGP and Kotlin in different PRs, so bisecting is trivial.
    • Keep the R8 rules next to the code that needs them (consumer rules in the data module), and track the merged configuration diff in review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): No global -keep class ** { *; } or -dontobfuscate. That gives up R8's shrinking, which is often a 20–40% dex reduction in apps that use it well (measure your own). I'd only leave full mode off as a short-lived flag, because full mode's extra optimizations are worth having. I wouldn't hand-roll rules for every model class if a codegen serializer migration is on the roadmap anyway.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does allowobfuscation on Retrofit interfaces not break it? → Retrofit reads annotations and generic signatures, not names. Renaming is fine as long as the attributes stay.
  • The crash shows fromJsonTyped$1 with "inlined" in the class name. Why? → The reified inline helper's anonymous TypeToken is regenerated in the caller's class per call site (Q144). That's also why keep rules must match * extends TypeToken, not a specific class.
  • Would kotlinx.serialization need Signature attributes? → Not for generated serializers resolved at compile time. Its library ships its own keep rules for the generated $serializer classes and companions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team found this two days before release, reverted the Kotlin upgrade on a hunch, still crashed, then shipped -dontobfuscate in panic. That leaked internal class names and grew the APK. The calm path took an afternoon: full-mode flag off, rules added, flag back on, verified on a minified CI build.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Reverts Kotlin, or proposes global keep/dontobfuscate.
  • Hire: Identifies R8 full mode (AGP 8 default) stripping Signature attributes, and adds targeted Gson/Retrofit rules.
  • Strong hire: Proves it with the full-mode toggle and APK inspection, upgrades libraries to bundled rules, adds a minified smoke test in CI, and recommends codegen serializers to remove the dependency on runtime signatures.

questions.promptHtml: What is a phantom type parameter, and how would you use one in Kotlin to make illegal states unrepresentable at compile time?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can use generics as a design tool, not just as containers. Phantom types are how seniors encode "validated vs unvalidated" or "builder step" rules in the type system without runtime checks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A phantom type parameter is a type parameter that appears in the class declaration but is never used in any field or member. It exists only to tag the type. For example, Id<User> and Id<Order> both wrap a String, but they're different types, so I can't pass an order id to a user lookup. I can also encode state: Form<Unvalidated> vs Form<Validated>, where submit() is only available as an extension on Form<Validated>. The tag is erased at runtime, so it costs nothing beyond the wrapper object, and if the wrapper is a @JvmInline value class it can often be free.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The tag type carries meaning only at compile time. Because it's unused in members, it can be declared out or in freely, with no position conflicts. Using it with variance is what makes hierarchies of tags work.

Id<User>     !=  Id<Order>          (invariant tag: no mixing)
Form<Validated> <: Form<Draft>?     only if Form is declared out S and Validated : Draft

Patterns:

  1. Typed ids. @JvmInline value class Id<T>(val raw: String). A value class can have a type parameter, and it is stored as just the String in most signatures. It boxes in the cases where any value class boxes (used as a generic T, nullable, Any). The value class chunk covers when it boxes, so don't rely on "zero cost" in generic collections like List<Id<User>>, which holds boxed objects.
  2. Type-state. Methods valid only in a state are extensions on that state:
sealed interface Draft
sealed interface Validated : Draft          // Validated is a Draft too

class Form<out S : Draft> internal constructor(val fields: Map<String, String>)

fun newForm(): Form<Draft> = Form(emptyMap())

fun Form<Draft>.validate(): Form<Validated>? =
    if ("email" in fields) Form(fields) else null

fun Form<Validated>.submit(api: Api) = api.post(fields)   // only compiles for validated forms
  1. Units/permissions. Money<USD> vs Money<EUR>, with operator fun plus(other: Money<C>) so adding mismatched currencies is a compile error.

Limits:

  • Nothing stops an as Form<Validated> cast. The compiler trusts it, so keep constructors internal or private and expose only validating factories.
  • Tags aren't visible at runtime, so you can't branch on them or serialize them. Serialization needs an explicit representation.
  • Overuse hurts readability: signatures like Repo<User, Remote, Cached> quickly become unreadable. Use it where a mix-up is expensive (ids, money, auth state).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@JvmInline value class Id<T>(val raw: String)

class User; class Order

fun loadUser(id: Id<User>): User = TODO()

val orderId = Id<Order>("o-1")
// loadUser(orderId)             // compile error: Id<Order> is not Id<User>
val userId = Id<User>("u-1")
loadUser(userId)                 // OK

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Making the tag a real constructor parameter "to be sure." Then it's not phantom, and you pay for it.
  • Exposing a public constructor of Form<Validated>, which bypasses the validation step.
  • Assuming a value class with a generic tag never boxes. It boxes in generic positions and when nullable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a phantom parameter be out without errors? → No member uses it in an in position, so there's nothing to violate.
  2. How do you serialize Id<User>? → As its underlying raw. kotlinx.serialization supports value classes, and the tag is re-attached by the declared type at the field.
  3. Why is this not just inheritance (UserId : Id)? → One generic class replaces N boilerplate classes, and generic code like fun <T> Id<T>.short() still works across all of them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "generic classes hold things of type T." The senior answer uses a generic parameter that holds nothing to move a runtime bug class (id mix-ups, skipped validation) to compile time, and states the limits (casts, boxing, readability).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fintech app had a bug where a String account id was passed as a transaction id to a refund API. After typed ids, the same mix-up became a compile error across 60 call sites.

questions.contextHtml:
You're defining the shared UI state type for 40 screens in a 25-engineer app. Current state: each screen has its own sealed class (OrdersState, ProfileState, ...), with duplicated loading/error handling, and a previous attempt at a shared type looked like this:

sealed class UiState<T> {
    class Loading<T> : UiState<T>()
    data class Success<T>(val data: T) : UiState<T>()
    data class Error<T>(val message: String) : UiState<T>()
}

Reported issues: every Loading() and Error() allocates an object, MutableStateFlow<UiState<Orders>> can't be assigned a UiState<Nothing>, mapping states needs unchecked casts (state as UiState<B>), and a screen needing "show cached data while refreshing" can't express it.
questions.promptHtml: Design the shared state type. Cover variance, mapping, what goes in the type vs outside, and how it behaves in a StateFlow.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sealed class with Loading, Success, Error, done." It leaves the type invariant, allocating, hard to map, and unable to express stale data plus an error.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do screens need data to survive loading/error (pull-to-refresh, offline)? (Common, and it decides the shape.) One-shot events: in or out of this type? (Out: separate concern.) Is the error user-facing text, a domain error, or a throwable? (Domain error type, mapped to text in UI.) Compose or Views, and is stability a concern? (Compose: yes, see below.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, so I'd skip an emergency fix. I'd ship the new type alongside the old ones and migrate screen by screen, with the old state classes unchanged.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (design options): (a) Shape A: Loading | Success(data) | Error as a sealed interface with out T. Simple, but loses data on refresh. (b) Shape B: one data class ScreenState<out T>(val data: T?, val isRefreshing: Boolean, val error: Error?). Expresses stale-with-error. But invalid combinations (data null and not loading and no error) are representable. (c) Shape C: sealed interface for the top-level lifecycle (Loading | Content | Failure), with Content holding data plus refreshing/transientError flags. Invalid states are mostly unrepresentable and stale data survives.
  4. How I'd verify each: Write the three real screens (list with pull-to-refresh, detail, form) against each shape and see which needs casts or flags. Unit test mapping and when exhaustiveness. Check Compose stability reports for the state classes.
  5. Root cause (of the old design's problems): The type parameter is invariant, so object states need a type parameter and can't be shared singletons. Making T out fixes it: Loading : UiState<Nothing> is a subtype of every UiState<X> (Q146). Mapping works because producers can be mapped without casts.
  6. Fix (design): 
    sealed interface UiState<out T> {
    data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>
    data class Failure(val error: AppError) : UiState<Nothing>
    data class Content<out T>(
        val data: T,
        val refreshing: Boolean = false,
        val refreshError: AppError? = null,   // stale data + error banner
    ) : UiState<T>
}

inline fun <T, R> UiState<T>.map(transform: (T) -> R): UiState<R> = when (this) {
    UiState.Loading -> UiState.Loading
    is UiState.Failure -> this
    is UiState.Content -> UiState.Content(transform(data), refreshing, refreshError)
}

// Usage in a ViewModel
private val _state = MutableStateFlow<UiState<Orders>>(UiState.Loading)
val state: StateFlow<UiState<Orders>> = _state.asStateFlow()
    Notes: StateFlow<out T> is covariant, so exposing StateFlow<UiState<Orders>> composes with UiState<out T>. MutableStateFlow stays invariant, hence MutableStateFlow<UiState<Orders>> with the exact type. data object needs Kotlin 1.9+ (on older versions use plain object).
  7. Prevention: Put the type and its map/fold helpers in one core module with tests. Document that events (navigation, snackbars) don't belong in UiState. A review rule: no as UiState<...> casts, since variance should make them unnecessary. For Compose, check stability: a Content holding a List<T> is treated as unstable by the compiler unless the strong skipping mode or an immutable collection (kotlinx.collections.immutable) is used. Check your Compose compiler version's behavior rather than assuming.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't use Kotlin's kotlin.Result<T> for UI state: it has no loading, it's meant for return values, and as a return type it required language flags in older Kotlin versions (verify for your version). I wouldn't make Failure carry a Throwable for screens to display, since that leaks implementation. I wouldn't add a fourth Empty state in the base type: emptiness is a content question (data.isEmpty()) that varies per screen.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why Failure : UiState<Nothing> and not Failure<T>? → There's no T value to carry, and an out hierarchy lets one object serve every T. If you later need "failure with last known data", that's Content.refreshError.
  • Does covariance matter for StateFlow equality and conflation? → Not directly. Content is a data class, so equal states are conflated. A list mutated in place won't be a new value, so copy it (separate chunk).
  • Can Content<out T> have a var? → No. A var data: T is an in position, so out would be rejected. That's a good constraint, since state should be immutable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a shared Resource<T> was invariant and allocated an Error<T> per recomposition-triggering update. Switching to out T plus singletons removed 40 as Resource<X> casts and made map helpers safe. The harder win was refreshError on Content, which killed the "blank screen on failed refresh" bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Invariant sealed class with three subclasses, no mapping or refresh story.
  • Hire: Covariant UiState<out T> with Nothing singletons, a map without casts, and asStateFlow() exposure.
  • Strong hire: Models stale data plus error, keeps events out, discusses Compose stability and migration path, and explains why kotlin.Result isn't the right tool.

questions.contextHtml:
Your team added a custom Retrofit CallAdapter.Factory so suspend APIs can return a sealed ApiResponse<T> instead of throwing. It works for ApiResponse<Unit> endpoints. For endpoints returning data, QA reports blank screens, and in staging logs:

E/ProfileVM: java.lang.ClassCastException: com.squareup.moshi.LinkedHashTreeMap...  (Moshi variant of the same problem)
   cannot be cast to com.app.profile.ProfileDto
E/Retrofit: Unable to create converter for class com.app.net.ApiResponse
   for method ProfileApi.getProfile

The factory:

sealed interface ApiResponse<out T> {
    data class Ok<T>(val body: T) : ApiResponse<T>
    data class HttpError(val code: Int) : ApiResponse<Nothing>
    data class NetworkError(val cause: java.io.IOException) : ApiResponse<Nothing>
}

class ApiResponseAdapterFactory : CallAdapter.Factory() {
    override fun get(returnType: Type, annotations: Array<Annotation>, retrofit: Retrofit): CallAdapter<*, *>? {
        if (getRawType(returnType) != Call::class.java) return null
        val inner = getParameterUpperBound(0, returnType as ParameterizedType)
        if (getRawType(inner) != ApiResponse::class.java) return null
        return ApiResponseCallAdapter<Any>(inner)             // BUG candidate
    }
}
class ApiResponseCallAdapter<T>(private val responseType: Type) : CallAdapter<T, Call<ApiResponse<T>>> {
    override fun responseType(): Type = responseType
    override fun adapt(call: Call<T>): Call<ApiResponse<T>> = ApiResponseCall(call)
}

The interface is suspend fun getProfile(): ApiResponse<ProfileDto>. Red herring: the backend returns slightly different JSON casing in staging.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and explain it in terms of generics and erasure. How do you fix and test it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The JSON casing is wrong," or "add a converter for ApiResponse." The first ignores the converter error, and the second works around the bug and puts parsing logic in the wrong place.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does ApiResponse<Unit> work because there's no body to parse? (Yes, and that's a clue.) Is the failure in debug and release? (Both: not R8.) What does Retrofit pass to Factory.get for a suspend function? (Call<ApiResponse<ProfileDto>>, since Retrofit models suspend functions as Call<T> for adapters.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pull the affected endpoints back to the plain Response<ProfileDto> return type behind a feature flag, or ship the one-line fix below if the test passes. No server action needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) responseType() returns ApiResponse<ProfileDto> where Retrofit expects the type of the HTTP body, ProfileDto. Matches "Unable to create converter for class ApiResponse." (b) Wrong factory order, so another adapter claims it first. Less likely given the message. (c) JSON casing. Wouldn't produce a converter-creation error.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log responseType() once per method: prints ApiResponse<ProfileDto>. Retrofit asks the converter factories for a Converter<ResponseBody, ApiResponse<ProfileDto>>, which Moshi/Gson then try to build as if ApiResponse were a JSON model, hence the converter error and the LinkedHashTreeMap on the lenient path. A MockWebServer unit test reproduces it in 10 lines.
  5. Root cause: CallAdapter.responseType() is the type that Retrofit's converter must produce from the response body. I passed the wrapper type, inner = ApiResponse<ProfileDto>, instead of its type argument. ApiResponse<Unit> worked because Unit/Void-style handling was special-cased. This is an erasure/reflection problem in disguise: the nested generic argument must be dug out of the ParameterizedType at runtime, since ApiResponseCallAdapter<Any> erases T, and the real type exists only as the Type object we pass in.
  6. Fix: 
    override fun get(returnType: Type, annotations: Array<Annotation>, retrofit: Retrofit): CallAdapter<*, *>? {
    if (getRawType(returnType) != Call::class.java) return null
    check(returnType is ParameterizedType) { "Call must be parameterized, e.g. Call<ApiResponse<Foo>>" }
    val wrapper = getParameterUpperBound(0, returnType)
    if (getRawType(wrapper) != ApiResponse::class.java) return null
    check(wrapper is ParameterizedType) { "ApiResponse must be parameterized" }
    val bodyType = getParameterUpperBound(0, wrapper)          // ProfileDto
    return ApiResponseCallAdapter<Any>(bodyType)
}
    ApiResponseCall.enqueue must also build Ok(body) from response.body() and map HttpException/IOException into the error subtypes, and handle Unit (204/empty body) explicitly. I'd write a MockWebServer test for ApiResponse<ProfileDto>, ApiResponse<List<ProfileDto>>, ApiResponse<Unit>, and HTTP 404, asserting the body types with assertIs.
  7. Prevention: The test matrix above runs in CI. The factory fails fast with check(...) messages at service creation instead of at call time. Keep the sealed type covariant (out T) so HttpError : ApiResponse<Nothing> is a singleton-friendly subtype, avoiding per-error casts (Q146).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't register a Converter.Factory for ApiResponse: parsing and error mapping are different concerns, and the converter would swallow HTTP errors. I wouldn't swallow all exceptions into NetworkError, since CancellationException must propagate when the coroutine is cancelled (see the cancellation chunk), and programmer errors shouldn't be disguised as network failures.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does Retrofit hand the adapter Call<ApiResponse<T>> for a suspend fun? → Retrofit's suspend support models the declared return type as a Call of it and then adapts, so adapter factories see the same shape as non-suspend code.
  • Would inline reified help in the factory? → No. The type arrives as a runtime Type from reflection of the interface method. There's no call site to substitute at. That's the "declaration signature survives erasure" case (Q150).
  • What if the endpoint returns ApiResponse<List<ProfileDto>>? → getParameterUpperBound(0, wrapper) returns the full ParameterizedType List<ProfileDto>, which the converter handles. Nothing extra is needed as long as the full Type is passed along, not a Class.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from several teams: the wrapper adapter passed all tests because every test endpoint returned Unit. The first data endpoint failed only in integration. A MockWebServer matrix test became the template for every future adapter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames JSON casing or adds a converter for the wrapper.
  • Hire: Spots that responseType() must be the body type and extracts it from the parameterized type.
  • Strong hire: Explains it as a runtime-Type (erasure) problem, adds fail-fast checks, a MockWebServer test matrix including List<T>, Unit, and error paths, and keeps cancellation semantics correct.

questions.subtopic: Variance and shared mutable generic state
questions.contextHtml:
A typed event bus lets modules publish and listen to events. After a refactor to "make it more flexible with variance", QA reports intermittent ClassCastException in the checkout module only when a promo banner is shown. Review the code:

open class AppEvent
class CartUpdated(val items: Int) : AppEvent()
class PromoShown(val code: String) : AppEvent()

class Bus<out E : AppEvent> {
    private val listeners = mutableListOf<(E) -> Unit>()           // private: not variance-checked

    fun listen(l: (@UnsafeVariance E) -> Unit) { listeners += l }  // "needed it to compile"
    fun publish(e: @UnsafeVariance E) { listeners.forEach { it(e) } }
}

val cartBus: Bus<CartUpdated> = Bus()
cartBus.listen { println("cart has ${it.items} items") }

val anyBus: Bus<AppEvent> = cartBus                                 // allowed because Bus is 'out'
anyBus.publish(PromoShown("SAVE10"))                                // compiles
java.lang.ClassCastException: com.app.PromoShown cannot be cast to com.app.CartUpdated
    at com.app.checkout.CheckoutKt$main$1.invoke(Checkout.kt:12)

Red herring: the stack mentions a lambda, and someone suspects R8 inlining.
questions.promptHtml: Why does this compile and crash, and how would you redesign the bus?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Catch the exception in publish," or "remove the lambda." Weak answers don't see that @UnsafeVariance hid a real soundness hole.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who publishes and who listens: the same module, or any? Do listeners ever need events of subtypes (a logger listening to all events)? Is it single-threaded? (Not relevant to this bug, but worth knowing.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the up-cast Bus<AppEvent> = cartBus usage in the promo path by publishing to a bus typed for promos, and revert the out modifier on Bus. Smallest safe diff.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Covariant Bus that takes E in publish. Fits perfectly: a PromoShown reaches a listener that expects CartUpdated. (b) R8 inlining. Debug repro, and the message names real classes, so no. (c) A threading race. It'd produce different symptoms and would not cause a wrong-type event.
  4. How I'd verify each: A 6-line JVM test reproduces it using the exact code above. Removing @UnsafeVariance shows the compile errors the annotation was hiding.
  5. Root cause: out E promises "this bus only produces E," but publish(e) and listen(l) consume E. The compiler flagged both. @UnsafeVariance silenced it, and the safe-to-annotate criterion (value not stored, not returned as E) is violated: publish hands the event to a stored (E) -> Unit. With the up-cast, the bus accepts any AppEvent and passes it to a listener that does it.items, and the compiler-inserted checkcast CartUpdated fails inside the lambda. The listeners list being private only hid the internal mismatch (private members aren't variance-checked).
  6. Fix: Split by role. Publishers need contravariance (a bus that accepts AppEvent can accept CartUpdated). Listeners want covariance of the event they receive from the source. 
    fun interface Listener<in E> { fun onEvent(e: E) }     // consumer of events

interface Publisher<in E> { fun publish(e: E) }        // can accept anything E or a subtype
interface Subscriber<out E> { fun listen(l: Listener<E>) }  // '− × −' = '+' : legal without annotation

class Bus<E : AppEvent> : Publisher<E>, Subscriber<E> {
    private val listeners = mutableListOf<Listener<E>>()
    override fun listen(l: Listener<E>) { listeners += l }
    override fun publish(e: E) { listeners.forEach { it.onEvent(e) } }
}

val cartBus = Bus<CartUpdated>()
val publishCart: Publisher<CartUpdated> = cartBus
val allPublisher: Publisher<AppEvent> = Bus<AppEvent>()
val cartSubscriber: Subscriber<AppEvent> = Bus<CartUpdated>()   // OK: Subscriber is out; listeners receive CartUpdated, which are AppEvents
    Better: callers get Publisher<CartUpdated> or Subscriber<CartUpdated> views of one invariant Bus<CartUpdated>. A single Bus<AppEvent> plus filterIsInstance-style typed subscription (inline fun <reified E : AppEvent> listen(...)) covers the "listen to a subtype" case without a lying cast.
  7. Prevention: A review rule: any @UnsafeVariance needs a comment proving the value is not stored or returned (Q147). Grep for it in CI as a flagged pattern. Unit tests that cast a Bus<Sub> to Bus<Base> and publish a sibling type.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't keep out and add runtime is checks in publish, which turns a compile-time guarantee into a runtime one and still lies in the type. I wouldn't wrap publish in try/catch, because it hides the heap pollution. I'd keep the invariant bus internal and expose the split role interfaces, which gives callers all the safe variance (Publisher<in E>, Subscriber<out E>).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is Subscriber<out E> with listen(l: Listener<E>) legal without an annotation? → Parameter (−) times Listener<in E> (−) is out (+). E is only produced to the listener (Q149).
  • Should I use SharedFlow<E> instead? → Probably. SharedFlow<out T> is covariant for collectors, and MutableSharedFlow<T> is invariant, which is the same split. It also gives lifecycle-aware collection and backpressure options.
  • Is listeners thread-safe? → No. Separate issue: add a CopyOnWriteArrayList or confine to one thread.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an analytics "typed" bus used @UnsafeVariance in four places "to satisfy the compiler." The team found it when a new event type crashed an unrelated listener at 2 a.m. The fix was a read/write split and removing all four annotations.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Wraps in try/catch or blames R8.
  • Hire: Identifies @UnsafeVariance hiding a real hole, because publish consumes E, and splits into role interfaces.
  • Strong hire: Also computes the nested positions correctly (Listener<in E> in a parameter is out), notes the private-member exemption concealed it, and suggests SharedFlow plus a review rule for @UnsafeVariance.
